Why Words Hurt Longer Than Physical Pain Words Cut Deep! Words can often hurt more and have longer-lasting effects than physical pain. That sentence used to sound dramatic to me. Now it just sounds accurate. A bruise fades on a predictable schedule. A sentence someone said to me a decade ago can still surface on an ordinary Tuesday, fully intact, as if no time passed at all. Physical pain has a biology to it that most of us understand instinctively. It signals damage, prompts healing, and eventually resolves. Emotional pain from words doesn’t follow that same timeline, and I think that’s exactly why it catches so many of us off guard. Why the Body Heals Faster Than the Mind Remembers A cut closes. A bone sets. The body has an entire system dedicated to repairing physical damage, efficiently and mostly without our conscious involvement. Words don’t get that same automatic repair process. They get stored, often in the exact tone and inflection they were delivered in, ready to replay themselves whenever something similar happens again. That’s the part that surprised me most. I can forget the specifics of a physical injury within weeks. I can still hear certain sentences, word for word, years after they were said, as clearly as the moment they landed. Words Attach Themselves to Identity, Not Just Moments Physical pain usually stays contained to the moment and the location it happened. Emotional pain from words tends to attach itself to something bigger, like how I see myself, what I believe I deserve, or what I expect from the people closest to me. A single sentence can quietly rewrite a belief that then shapes decisions for years afterward. That’s a much larger footprint than a bruise ever leaves. A physical injury doesn’t usually change how you interpret your own worth. The right words, said at the right moment of vulnerability, absolutely can. Why We Still Underestimate Verbal Harm There’s a strange cultural habit of treating physical harm as automatically more serious than verbal harm, maybe because physical harm leaves visible evidence and verbal harm doesn’t. “It’s just words” gets said far too often, as if the absence of a mark on the skin means the absence of real damage underneath it. I’ve stopped agreeing with that framing. Some of the deepest wounds I carry didn’t come from anything physical at all. They came from sentences said by people who mattered to me, in moments when I was least prepared to defend myself against them. The Replay Effect That Physical Pain Doesn’t Have Physical pain rarely replays itself involuntarily once it’s healed. Words do. A specific phrase, tone, or context can trigger the exact same emotional response years later, even when the person who said it is long gone from my life. That replay effect is unique to verbal wounds, and it’s part of why they can outlast almost anything physical. I’ve had to learn to recognize when I’m in a replay instead of a present-moment reaction. That distinction alone has helped me respond to old words with more clarity than I used to. What Healing From Words Actually Requires Healing a bruise mostly requires time and rest. Healing from words requires something more active. It requires noticing the belief a sentence planted, questioning whether it’s actually true, and slowly replacing it with something more accurate. That’s a longer, more deliberate process than most physical healing ever demands. It also usually requires new words, spoken by people who actually see you clearly, to compete with the old ones and eventually take up more space in your mind than they do. Why This Changes How I Speak to Others Now Once I understood how long words can live inside someone, I got a lot more careful with mine. I try to remember that whatever I say in a heated moment might outlast the moment itself by years. That awareness has made me slower to speak in anger and quicker to choose words that won’t need years of undoing later. Where This Leaves Me Words can often hurt and have longer lasting effects than physical pain. I believe that fully now, not as a dramatic statement but as something I’ve lived through directly. The bruises fade. Some sentences never fully do. Knowing that has changed both how I protect myself from words and how carefully I choose the ones I offer to everyone else. happiness mentalHealth personalGrowth quotes relationships

Be patient with in your heart and try to love the questions themselves THE PSYCHOLOGY OF SCARCITY 20 Themes on Competition, Resources, Human Behaviour and the Future of Survival PLNNABLOG Magazine | Psychology • Evolution • Economics • Society • Technology By Joshua Shipepe Hadula 10 What happens to the human mind when people believe there is not enough to go around? Scarcity can change how people think about money, employment, food, land, status, education, political power and even their relationships. When a resource becomes limited—or is perceived to be limited—people may become more competitive, protective, inventive, cooperative or fearful. This is not a single, universal psychological response. Human behaviour depends on the resource, the level of threat, cultural expectations, institutional trust and whether people believe the system is fair. The central question for this PLNNABLOG feature is: Does competition over resources bring out humanity’s strongest survival instincts, or can it trap societies in cycles of anxiety, inequality and conflict? The following 20 themes explore the psychology behind that question, from evolutionary survival to artificial intelligence and economic opportunity. The 20 themes 1. The scarcity mindset: when survival takes over thinking When money, food, time or employment feels insufficient, attention can narrow towards immediate needs. A 2024 meta-analysis covering 29 datasets and 111,852 respondents found an overall negative association between financial scarcity and cognitive performance, although effects can vary by context and task. ScienceDirect +1 Central question: How can people make long-term plans when daily survival consumes their attention? 2. The zero-sum mindset: your success, my loss People sometimes believe that another person’s gain must automatically reduce their own opportunities. Psychology calls this a zero-sum belief. It can appear in employment, business, politics and international relations—even when cooperation could create additional value. Nature Reviews Psychology +1 Central question: Are people competing over genuinely limited resources, or over a belief that resources cannot grow? 3. Employment competition and the psychology of rejection When many applicants pursue a few vacancies, rejection can feel like a judgement of personal worth. In reality, hiring also depends on qualifications, timing, budgets and organisational needs. Central question: How can societies make employment competition fair without making unemployment a source of permanent social exclusion? 4. Status anxiety and social comparison People compare income, possessions, professional titles and lifestyles. Social comparison can motivate improvement, but it can also generate shame, envy and endless dissatisfaction when success is measured only against others. Central question: Can ambition exist without turning every other person’s progress into a personal threat? 5. Fear of losing what we already have Losing a job, home, savings or social position can feel more threatening than an equivalent potential gain feels rewarding. Loss aversion is one concept used to explain this pattern, although its strength varies between decisions and people. Central question: How does fear of loss shape financial choices, business decisions and willingness to innovate? 6. Water, land and the psychology of survival Water and land are physical resources with real limits. Competition can become intense when access is unequal, livelihoods are threatened or institutions cannot resolve disputes fairly. Yet communities can also cooperate to manage shared resources. Annual Reviews +1 Central question: What turns environmental pressure into conflict—and what allows it to become collective problem-solving? 7. Cooperation versus competition Scarcity does not automatically make people selfish. Depending on trust, social expectations and the situation, it can increase helping behaviour or reduce it. Research reviews caution against assuming a single universal response. ScienceDirect +1 Central question: Which social conditions encourage people to share risk rather than fight over limited supplies? 8. Trust, fairness and the rules of competition People may tolerate unequal outcomes more readily when they believe the process is fair, transparent and open to participation. Perceptions of favouritism can undermine trust even when resources are available. Central question: How do fair recruitment, transparent procurement and accountable leadership change competitive behaviour? 9. Education as a competition for future security Education can open economic opportunities, but limited scholarships, training places and jobs can turn learning into a high-pressure race. When qualifications become the only recognised route to success, practical talent may be overlooked. Central question: How can education create capability without making every examination feel like a fight for survival? 10. Mental health under permanent competition Constant pressure to outperform others can contribute to stress, exhaustion and feelings of inadequacy. The effect depends on workload, resources, personal circumstances and available support. Central question: How can organisations reward excellence without making rest, health and dignity appear to be weaknesses? 11. Social media and the competition for attention Online platforms expose people to curated images of wealth, achievement and popularity. This can distort perceptions of how others actually live and encourage continuous comparison. Central question: Are digital platforms helping people discover opportunities—or intensifying the feeling that everyone else is winning? 12. Entrepreneurship: turning competition into value creation Businesses can compete for customers, but they can also create new products, improve services and reach previously underserved markets. This shifts the focus from dividing existing wealth to developing useful value. Central question: What unmet needs can entrepreneurs solve instead of entering markets only to imitate established competitors? 13. AI and the fear of becoming economically replaceable PLNNABLOG_Scarcity_to_Opportunity_Patent_Concept_Joshua_Shipepe_Hadula Download Automation can reduce demand for some tasks while creating new tasks and opportunities elsewhere. The transition can be difficult for workers whose experience does not match emerging job requirements. Central question: How can societies distribute the gains from AI while helping workers adapt and preserving meaningful employment? 14. The unequal distribution of technological opportunity Access to devices, reliable internet, training, capital and professional networks affects who can benefit from technological change. Equal access to a tool does not always produce equal outcomes. Central question: How can Namibia turn digital development into practical opportunities for people outside established economic networks? 15. Community cooperation and shared resources Cooperatives, shared equipment, community water systems and joint purchasing can lower costs and spread risk. Such arrangements need clear rules, accountability and ways to resolve disputes. Central question: Which resources are better managed collectively than individually? 16. National competition for minerals, energy and influence Countries compete for investment, energy security, strategic minerals and market access. Resource abundance can create opportunities, but governance, revenue distribution and accountability influence whether benefits reach citizens. Research finds that the relationship between resources and conflict varies with context. ScienceDirect +1 Central question: How can resource-rich African countries negotiate for long-term development rather than short-term advantage alone? 17. Fear, uncertainty and the psychology of the future When people cannot predict whether employment, prices or housing will improve, they may delay investment, avoid risks or favour immediate security. Others respond by experimenting and diversifying. Central question: How can reliable information and social protection help people make decisions under uncertainty? 18. Nonlinear opportunity: the unexpected route to success Economic progress does not always follow a straight path from education to employment to promotion. A side project, new skill, partnership or small experiment can open an unexpected route. Central question: How can people test ideas at low cost and discover opportunities without risking everything at once? 19. Generational competition and the social contract Younger people may feel excluded from housing, secure employment or capital, while older generations may fear losing pensions, savings or established security. Treating this as a battle between age groups can hide shared structural problems. Central question: How can housing, skills and employment policies create opportunities across generations rather than pit them against each other? 20. From scarcity to resilience: redesigning the competition The final theme asks whether institutions can reduce unnecessary competition by improving access to essentials, strengthening trust, supporting innovation and managing shared resources responsibly. Central question: What would an economy look like if success meant not only winning individually, but also making more people secure enough to contribute? The central psychological model Resource pressure Money • Jobs • Land • Water • Status Psychological interpretation Threat • Fairness • Trust • Perceived opportunity Defensive response Hoarding, exclusion, distrust or conflict Constructive response Cooperation, innovation, sharing or adaptation A conceptual framework, not a deterministic law. Real outcomes depend on individual differences, institutions and circumstances. Research on zero-sum beliefs suggests that perceived threat, scarcity and reduced opportunity for deliberation can encourage people to interpret other groups’ gains as their own losses. Yet cooperation remains possible, especially when trust and shared interests are supported. Nature Reviews Psychology +1 What this means for Namibia For Namibia, the framework could be applied to competition over jobs, housing, land, education, access to finance, water and emerging digital opportunities. The practical response is not to tell people to stop competing. It is to ask whether the rules of competition are transparent, whether people have a realistic chance to participate, and whether collective investment can expand the opportunities available. Possible priorities include: Skills programmes linked to actual employer and market demand. Transparent recruitment and procurement processes. Affordable access to digital tools and business information. Stronger mental-health support in high-pressure workplaces and learning environments. Community-based approaches to managing scarce resources. Support for small experiments that help people test business ideas before taking large financial risks. These are policy directions to evaluate, not guaranteed solutions. Their effectiveness depends on implementation, resources and evidence of outcomes. Conclusion: the greatest competition is over the conditions of survival Human beings compete because resources, opportunities and status can be limited. But people also cooperate, invent, share knowledge and create new forms of value. The psychological danger begins when competition becomes the only way people understand society—when another person’s progress is automatically interpreted as a threat, and when scarcity becomes a permanent expectation even where cooperation could improve outcomes. The opportunity is to build systems in which people can compete fairly while still trusting one another enough to cooperate. The goal is not a world without competition. It is a world where competition encourages capability and innovation without destroying mental well-being, social trust or the possibility of shared prosperity. Perhaps the answer begins with remembering the child we once were. 1. Introduction: The child we left behind Add to Favorites ergsy There is a stage in life when the world seems full of possibilities. A child can ask a hundred questions in one afternoon, turn an ordinary object into a toy, imagine becoming a scientist, and believe that tomorrow might bring something wonderful. Then something changes. We begin comparing ourselves with others. We become embarrassed by our mistakes. We worry about what people think. We learn to hide our uncertainty behind confidence, silence, anger, or even arrogance. Some of us become afraid to try. Others become afraid to look weak. Relearning how to be an eleven-year-old kid is an invitation to examine what we have lost while growing up—and what we can recover without abandoning the responsibilities of adulthood. This is not a call to behave irresponsibly or to pretend that childhood was perfect. Some children experience painful circumstances, exclusion, bullying, instability, or responsibilities far beyond their years. Childhood is not equally safe for everyone. Instead, this is a conversation about restoring the qualities that help human beings grow: curiosity, play, humility, emotional honesty, courage and the willingness to learn. 2. Arrogance: When the fear of being wrong becomes a wall Add to Favorites Arrogance is often mistaken for confidence. Yet confidence and arrogance are not the same. Confidence allows a person to say, “I can try.” Humility allows a person to say, “I might be wrong.” Arrogance insists, “I already know.” A child who fears embarrassment may pretend to understand a lesson rather than ask the teacher to explain it again. An adult may reject constructive criticism because accepting it threatens their public image. A leader may surround themselves with people who agree with them instead of people who challenge their assumptions. In each case, the desire to protect one’s image can become more important than the opportunity to learn. But there is an important distinction: arrogance is a behaviour, not an identity. A person who behaves arrogantly is not necessarily incapable of humility. The behaviour can be recognised, questioned and changed. The lesson from an eleven-year-old is simple: you do not have to know everything to have value. The willingness to ask a question is not proof of weakness. It is evidence that learning is still possible. 3. Fear: The invisible classroom Add to Favorites Fear does not always look like trembling or crying. Sometimes fear looks like perfectionism. Sometimes it looks like procrastination. Sometimes it looks like refusing to participate, laughing at someone else’s mistake, or pretending that an opportunity was never important. A learner may fear answering incorrectly in front of classmates. A young professional may fear applying for a position because rejection feels unbearable. A person with a promising idea may never share it because someone might criticise it. Fear can protect us from genuine danger. But when the possibility of embarrassment begins controlling every decision, it can prevent growth. The answer is not to eliminate every feeling of fear. It is to learn how to act thoughtfully while fear is present. Ask yourself: What am I afraid people will discover about me? Am I protecting myself from genuine harm, or from the discomfort of being a beginner? What would I attempt if making a mistake did not mean losing my worth? Who could help me feel safe enough to try? You do not have to answer every question immediately. Sometimes courage begins with admitting that you are afraid. 4. The relationship between arrogance and fear Add to Favorites soulshoppe Arrogance and fear may appear to be opposites, but they can sometimes serve the same purpose: protecting a person from feeling exposed. Fear says, “I do not want anyone to see me fail.” Arrogance says, “I cannot be seen as someone who fails.” One person withdraws from the challenge. Another attacks the challenge, dismisses the teacher or blames others. These are possible responses, not universal explanations. Arrogance can also come from entitlement, learned social behaviour or a desire for power. Fear can arise from real danger and previous experiences. Nevertheless, recognising the connection can help us respond more constructively. When fear takes overWhen arrogance takes overA healthier response“I cannot do this.”“I already know this.”“Let me try and learn.”Avoiding questionsDismissing questionsListening with curiosityHiding mistakesBlaming othersTaking responsibilityComparing ourselvesLooking down on othersRespecting different abilitiesGiving up after criticismRejecting all criticismExamining useful feedback The goal is not to become timid or to abandon confidence. It is to develop confidence that does not depend on pretending to be perfect. 5. What does an eleven-year-old teach us about learning? Add to Favorites note At eleven, a child is still developing their understanding of friendship, fairness, identity, responsibility and the wider world. Children differ greatly in their maturity, circumstances and abilities, so there is no single way every eleven-year-old thinks or behaves. Still, this stage offers an opportunity to reflect on several essential learning habits. Curiosity: asking why something happens instead of simply accepting it. Experimentation: trying a different approach when the first attempt fails. Feedback: listening to guidance and deciding how to use it. Social learning: discovering that other people may see a problem differently. Persistence: recognising that improvement often requires practice. The American Psychological Association’s educational resources explain that students who adopt a growth-oriented view of learning tend to approach challenges more willingly and recover more readily from setbacks. The emphasis is on improvement through effort, useful strategies and feedback—not on pretending that effort alone guarantees success. American Psychological Association +1 Imagine returning to a classroom as an adult. You do not need to compete with the youngest learner. You need to recover the willingness to say, “Please explain that again.” The best learner is not necessarily the person who answers first. It is the person who remains willing to understand. 6. The child who wanted to play Add to Favorites gofundme Play is often dismissed as something people outgrow. Once employment, bills, deadlines and family responsibilities arrive, enjoyment can begin to feel like a reward that must be earned. But play can serve purposes beyond entertainment. It can create opportunities for social connection, imagination, emotional expression and experimentation. UNICEF’s parenting resources discuss how play can help children process difficult emotions and how supportive play experiences can help buffer the effects of stress. UNICEF Parenting For an adult, relearning how to play might mean kicking a football with friends, learning to draw, gardening, dancing, reading a comic book or exploring a new hobby. It does not mean ignoring responsibilities. It means recognising that a life devoted entirely to obligations can leave little space for joy. You are allowed to enjoy something without turning it into a business, a competition or a measure of your success. 7. The importance of being heard Add to Favorites linkedin Imagine a child asking a question and being laughed at. Imagine a learner admitting that they do not understand a lesson, only to be told that they should already know the answer. Imagine a young person trying to explain a feeling and being interrupted before finishing the first sentence. Repeated experiences like these can discourage a person from speaking openly. They do not determine every person’s future, but they can influence whether someone feels safe enough to ask for help. The Harvard University Center on the Developing Child describes responsive, back-and-forth interactions between children and caring adults as important for developing communication, social skills and healthy foundations for learning. Harvard Center on Developing Child +1 This has implications for parents, teachers, schools and communities. A child does not need every answer to be correct. A child needs an environment in which questions can be explored, mistakes can be addressed constructively, and difficult feelings can be discussed safely. Adults need these conditions, too. Sometimes relearning childhood means finding people who listen without humiliating us—and learning to offer that same respect to others. 8. Education: Correcting mistakes without destroying confidence Add to Favorites A classroom can teach more than the content printed in a textbook. It can teach a learner that mistakes are part of learning, or that mistakes invite humiliation. It can encourage curiosity, or reward only those who already know the answers. Consider two responses to a learner who gives an incorrect answer. The first response is: “You should know this by now. Were you not listening?” The second is: “Let’s examine how you reached that answer. Which step should we revisit?” Both responses address the mistake, but the second creates a clearer path towards understanding. This does not mean that teachers should abandon standards or avoid correcting learners. It means that correction should help learners improve rather than make them feel that their worth is defined by one performance. The same principle applies in workplaces, universities, families and public institutions. Accountability and kindness are not enemies. We can correct errors without humiliating the person who made them. For Namibia, this conversation is relevant wherever young people are learning under pressure, whether in crowded classrooms, vocational institutions, universities or community programmes. The objective should be to develop people who can think independently, accept correction, ask meaningful questions and contribute to society. 9. Social media and the performance of being grown-up Add to Favorites maenner Today’s children encounter a world in which popularity, appearance and achievement can be measured publicly through likes, views, comments and followers. Adults face similar pressures. We may begin performing confidence instead of developing it. We may display success while concealing uncertainty. We may mistake being admired for being understood. Social media is not inherently harmful, and it can provide community, education and creativity. The concern is what happens when public approval becomes the primary measure of personal worth. A useful question is: If nobody could see my achievements, would I still want to pursue them? Another is: Can I appreciate someone else’s success without interpreting it as evidence of my own failure? An eleven-year-old mindset, at its best, leaves room to explore an interest before deciding whether it will impress anyone. Sometimes the healthiest thing you can do is learn something privately, practise without announcing it, and allow yourself to improve away from the public eye. 10. Humility is not weakness Add to Favorites Humility is often misunderstood as thinking less of yourself. A healthier understanding is being able to recognise both your strengths and your limitations without needing to place yourself above other people. A humble person can lead confidently, disagree respectfully, accept praise, acknowledge mistakes and learn from someone younger or less experienced. Humility does not require accepting abuse, remaining silent about injustice or surrendering your boundaries. It means that your dignity does not depend on proving that everyone else is inferior. Try these four habits: Listen before responding. Make sure you understand what the other person means. Admit what you do not know. Uncertainty is an opportunity to investigate. Apologise when necessary. Take responsibility without turning the apology into an excuse. Give credit fairly. Recognise the contributions and knowledge of other people. You do not become smaller by learning from someone else. You become more capable of seeing the world beyond yourself. 11. When childhood was not safe Add to Favorites There is an important qualification to the idea of returning to childhood. Not everyone remembers being eleven as a happy time. Some people experienced bullying, grief, family conflict, neglect, discrimination or circumstances that required them to become responsible too early. Others may have felt that they had to be perfect to receive approval. For these people, the phrase “be a child again” may bring sadness rather than comfort. Relearning how to be eleven does not mean romanticising what happened or forcing yourself to forgive someone who harmed you. It may mean recognising what you needed at that age: protection, encouragement, friendship, stability or permission to make mistakes. It may mean setting boundaries now, talking with a trusted person, seeking professional support when needed, or allowing yourself to enjoy safe experiences without feeling guilty. You cannot change the past. But the past does not have to dictate every opportunity you allow yourself in the present. You do not have to recreate your childhood to recover the parts of yourself that still deserve care. 12. What developmental experts can teach us The following institutions offer evidence-based resources relevant to childhood, learning and emotional development. Add to Favorites Harvard University — Center on the Developing Child Its work examines how relationships, environments and experiences influence development. Its research-informed resources are useful for understanding why supportive relationships matter. Explore: developingchild.harvard.edu Add to Favorites American Psychological Association (APA) Its educational psychology resources discuss motivation, feedback, learning beliefs and how classroom practices can influence learners’ willingness to attempt challenging work. Explore: apa.org/ed/schools Add to Favorites UNICEF — Child Development and Parenting Its resources address play, supportive relationships and children’s emotional well-being, providing useful material for parents, educators and communities. Explore: unicef.org/parenting These resources support the broader argument that healthy development involves relationships, opportunities to learn, and environments that encourage growth. They do not establish that arrogance always originates in fear or that every adult should seek to recreate childhood. Those are questions for personal reflection, not universal psychological diagnoses. Harvard Center on Developing Child +2 13. The seven-day challenge: Begin again Add to Favorites You do not need a dramatic life change to begin. Start with small actions that help you practise curiosity, courage and kindness. Your personal reset 0/7 days Monday — Ask Ask one genuine question about something you do not understand. Tuesday — Play Make time for an activity you enjoy without needing to be good at it. Wednesday — Listen Listen to another person’s perspective without preparing an immediate rebuttal. Thursday — Try Attempt something you have avoided because you fear making a mistake. Friday — Repair Where appropriate, apologise for a mistake or acknowledge someone’s contribution. Saturday — Explore Visit a park, read about a new subject, draw, cook or explore nature. Sunday — Reflect Write down what you learned, what frightened you and what you want to try next. At the end of the week, ask yourself whether you became more willing to learn, more honest about your feelings, or more comfortable admitting uncertainty. The goal is not to become a perfect person in seven days. It is to practise a different way of responding to yourself and others. 14. A letter to the eleven-year-old inside us Add to Favorites medium Dear eleven-year-old me, I am sorry for the times I believed I had to know everything to be respected. I am sorry for the moments when I was afraid to ask questions, afraid to fail, or afraid that someone might discover I was still learning. I am learning that I do not need to pretend to be fearless. I do not need to win every argument. I do not need to make other people feel small to feel important. I can be confident without being arrogant. I can be afraid and still take a thoughtful step forward. I can accept correction without losing my dignity. I can be serious about my responsibilities and still laugh, play, dream and explore. I cannot return to the day I was eleven. But I can give myself permission to keep learning, to build healthier relationships and to treat the person I am becoming with compassion. I hope I never become so proud that I stop listening, or so afraid that I stop trying. With patience and courage, The person you are still becoming. 15. Conclusion: Growing older without losing your humanity Add to Favorites trish-ingels Perhaps maturity is not the process of eliminating every childish quality. Perhaps it is learning which qualities deserve to grow with us. Keep the curiosity that asks questions. Keep the courage that attempts difficult things. Keep the imagination that sees possibilities beyond current circumstances. Keep the humility that recognises other people have something to teach you. And keep enough emotional honesty to acknowledge fear without allowing it to make every decision. Arrogance may protect an image, but humility creates room for growth. Fear may warn us about danger, but courage helps us distinguish real risks from the discomfort of learning something new. The world does not need adults who know everything. It needs adults who are willing to listen, question, learn, correct their mistakes and treat other people with dignity. You do not have to become eleven again. You have to remember that the person you are today is still allowed to learn. Living IN the moment (and not for the trend!) I am not sure whether I should say this out loud or not, but I think I must. If there is anyone out there, who thinks that there is no such thing as beginning again, I can tell you with total assurance that I know now that tuning your heart to your present is eventually the path that will help. I don’t know how I found the strength to get up and change my life, but traveling to a beautiful village tucked away in the heart of Dharamshala brought me the peace and comfort that I desperately needed. I spent more than 100 days away from the city that I call home. I don’t know why I was not able to function normally for so many years that I spent at home. But, getting some distance from the family that has been there all along was this impossible, but really urgent thing….something that I had to do. I just had to do. Did I want a second chance? Hell, yes. Did I think I was going to get it? No. Did I really break my heart, trying to heal myself? Yes. It wasn’t in my hands. I had to trust higher powers for it. What did I learn after spending so many days living alone and figuring out my problems? A LOT. I learned that none of it was in my hands…that the struggle was something that I had to go through, in order to change. I learned that I am still too young to take on so much pain and regret for things that happen to the best of us. I learned that it is time to let go, and live the life that calls out to me. What did I go through, really? Well, I isolated myself from things that irked me and pissed me off more than they should. Anyone who smiled or seemed to enjoy without a care in the world really bothered me, and I just couldn’t understand why I wasn’t able to take it easy. I became a grandma, without wanting to become one. Then, something changed, and I was challenged by the universe to question my ways. Opinion before the trip: you can do what you want in life, and not just once…always. Opinion after the trip: you can do what you want in life, and not just once…always…but it comes with a lot of hard work and sacrifice. You can easily become free, and lose your way too. Post my trip to Dharamshala, I was excited to see if I had really changed my ways. So, I took up a content shoot project away from the city I live in. I wanted to experience the change myself that I had experienced when I was in the mountains. Once I started out though, I realised that I had definitely grown calmer and more relaxed. I was less scared of the future, of the many ways that I could go wrong with my life and I just couldn’t care about the fact that…hey, what now? I almost surprised me. But, once I came back home, after 5 months…I freaked out. I didn’t think that I could really carry on the pursuit as I wished.. This time, life was in my face again. It asked me: am I willing to put in the work and correct my vision? Am I ready to continue keeping my head down and do the work? In a world where anyone and everyone can get up and test our willpower, is it really my responsibility to protect my freedom? Hell yes. I don’t know why I am in awe, and afraid of where our world is going. But I know that it is a fear that many of us share these days. All of us want to figure this out our way, and I guess that is totally fine, isn’t it? We weren’t born to follow just one kind of system. What we do with our freedom is our call. My travel trip to Dharamshala and another secret city have changed me for the better. Travel has always healed me in ways that I cannot explain. But Dharamshala really really opened my heart, allowed me to shed old baggage and start afresh. If you have never been to Dharamshala, please…book that trip now, and go.

You know the moment. You're waiting for the kettle, or the elevator, or a page to load, or a friend who's running late. There's a gap — thirty seconds, maybe three — of nothing to do. And your hand is in your pocket before you've even decided to reach for it. Not because you need anything. There's no message you're waiting on, nothing urgent. It's closer to a flinch — a small, automatic recoil from the empty moment, like the quiet is something to be escaped rather than simply stood in. I do it constantly. I'd guess you do too. Here's what caught me up short recently: I tried to remember the last time I was genuinely bored. Not "between tasks," not "scrolling because I'm avoiding something" — actually bored. No screen, no input, no stream of someone else's thoughts pouring into mine. Just me, and an unfilled stretch of time, and nothing to fill it with. I couldn't remember. It might have been years. And for most of my life, I'd have called that a win. Boredom was the enemy, right? The thing to be solved, optimized away, never tolerated. We finally killed it. We have, in our pockets, an infinite supply of things to never be bored with again. I'm starting to think we lost something, and I didn't notice it leaving. Boredom was never empty Here's the reframe that's been sitting with me. I always thought of boredom as empty time — dead air, wasted minutes, the absence of anything happening. But that's not what it was. Boredom was the one mode where your mind got to wander with no destination. Where it drifted, made odd connections, chewed on things in the background, daydreamed its way into ideas you weren't trying to have. It looked like nothing was happening. Underneath, a lot was. Think about where your actual good ideas come from. Not the ones you grind out at a desk — the real ones, the ones that arrive sideways. They come in the shower. On a walk with no podcast. Staring out a train window. In the drifting minutes before sleep. "Shower thought" is a cliché precisely because it's true : insight shows up in the gaps, not in the grind. The gaps were when your brain finally had room to connect the dots it had been quietly collecting all day. Boredom was the soil those ideas grew in. We just called it wasted time, because it didn't look productive — and so, the moment we had a way to eliminate it, we did. We filled every gap, and barely noticed What's strange is that nobody chose this. There was no moment where you decided, "I will never again sit in an empty minute." It just happened, gradually, one filled gap at a time. The commute got filled. The waiting room got filled. The queue at the shop, the ad break, the walk from the car, the thirty seconds for the kettle — all of it, filled. There is now no idle moment in a normal day that has to stay idle, because there's always something within reach to pour into it. And because the filler is so good — endlessly novel, perfectly tuned — the reaching became automatic. You don't decide to fill the gap. The gap appears and the hand moves. It got paved over so quietly that the loss never registered as a loss. You don't miss the shower thoughts you didn't have. You don't notice the ideas that didn't connect because the dots never got their idle time together. The mental space didn't get taken from you in some dramatic way you'd resent. It got nibbled, a moment at a time, until there was none left and you'd forgotten it was ever there. And now there's a new filler, and it's the most seductive one yet The feed was one thing. At least with a feed you still had to do a little of the work — scroll, choose, react, think something. But there's a newer gap we've started filling, and it's a quieter, deeper one: not knowing. You used to be allowed to not know things for a while. You'd hit a question and have to sit with it — turn it over on the walk home, stay puzzled through dinner, wake up still chewing on it. That unresolved state was uncomfortable, and it was also doing something. Sitting with a question is how you actually think about it. The puzzlement was the processing. Now the answer is instant. You wonder something, you ask, it's there. Which is genuinely wonderful, and I use it all day. But it means the puzzlement never gets to happen anymore. The question and the answer have collapsed into the same second, and the thinking that used to live in the space between them has nowhere to occur. And I notice this is the same shape as something I wrote about before — the way the struggle of solving a hard problem yourself was where the satisfaction lived, and removing the struggle quietly removed the joy. This is the twin of that. First we optimized away the friction of struggling . Now we're optimizing away the friction of not knowing , and of being unoccupied . We keep finding the uncomfortable mental states and smoothing them out — and it keeps turning out that the discomfort was load-bearing. The friction was where the good stuff lived. What I think we actually lost It's easy to make this about "attention spans," but I don't think that's quite it, and that framing lets us off too easy. The loss is more specific, and more human. We lost the ideas that only come in the gaps. If there's never an unfilled moment, there's never a shower thought. We may be quietly starving our own creativity — not because we got less creative, but because creativity needs idle, undirected time to do its work, and we deleted the idle time. We lost being alone with our own minds. Boredom used to force a kind of self-contact — your own unmediated thoughts, with nothing in between. Fill every gap and you can get through an entire day without once being truly alone with your mind. There's a strange new loneliness in that: never lonely, because never without input, and also never actually with yourself. We lost our tolerance for discomfort. The flinch toward the phone in the empty three seconds is really a shrinking ability to sit in any unstructured, uncomfortable moment. And that tolerance was quietly holding up a lot of other things — patience, deep focus, the capacity to stay with a hard problem long enough to crack it. You can't do deep work if you can't tolerate thirty seconds of nothing. I don't have a fix, and I'm suspicious of anyone who does This is the part where a post like this usually pivots to "so do a digital detox!" and gives you a five-step plan. I'm not going to, because I don't believe it, and I think you'd feel the hollowness of it. The honest situation is harder than that. You can't really go back — the gaps are filled, the tools exist and they're genuinely useful, and "just be bored on purpose" turns out to be weirdly difficult, because you always know relief is one tap away. Boredom you could escape at any second isn't really boredom; it's a test of willpower, which is a different and more tiring thing. Manufactured idleness isn't the same as the real kind, the same way choosing a hard path when the easy one is right there isn't the same as having no choice. And it isn't all bad. The filled commute, the instant answer, the never-dull waiting room — these are real conveniences, and I'm not going to pretend I'd hand them back. This isn't a lament for a better past. It's just an honest noticing: we traded something we didn't know we needed for something obviously convenient, and we can't cleanly un-trade it. We got rid of boredom without ever asking what boredom was for. So Here's the only thing I'll offer, and it's small on purpose. Next time you're waiting for the kettle, try not reaching. Just stand there in the empty thirty seconds and notice what your mind does when you take it off the leash. It'll feel uncomfortable — faintly itchy, like you're forgetting to do something. That discomfort is the thing. It's the muscle we stopped using, twitching because it hasn't been asked to work in years. We didn't lose boredom. We evicted it — quietly, conveniently, one filled moment at a time. And it's only now, in the rare second the room goes quiet, that some of us are realizing boredom had been paying rent all along, on something we actually miss: the wandering, the connecting, the just-being-with-ourselves. We filled the room with noise and only noticed the furniture was gone once it got quiet enough to look. I don't know how to get it back. But I think I want to try to be bored again, at least sometimes. On purpose. Badly. Starting with the kettle. Honest question, and I'd love real answers: when's the last time you were truly bored — no phone, no screen, no AI, just an empty moment you didn't fill? I struggled to remember mine, and I don't think I'm the only one. How Soon Is Now? 6–9 minutes I wasted almost ten minutes of my life this morning… time I’ll never get back! I was trying to prove to a website that I am not a (enter expletive of choice!) robot! I clicked on every blurry square containing a (more swear words!) “hydrant” until my eyes were crossed and my fuse was blown! It’s another 21st-century glitch: we spend our days proving our humanity to a mindless interface, only to spend our evenings trying to find human connection… inside another one. If you’ve been following my Citizen Jane Field Guides™️ , you’ll know I’ve been railing against the Syndicate – those 10 global giants that want to own your pantry and your plate. But now, they’ve set their sights on something much more valuable (and far more sinister). They’ve started mining our loneliness. And in 2026, business is booming…. I. The Silicon Soulmate 📱💘 There’s a specific kind of quiet that’s settled over the world in recent years. Whether you’re in a pub in Glasgow or a coffee shop in Seattle, look around you. Half the people are “connected” to someone who doesn’t actually exist . We’re seeing a massive rise in “ AI Companions ” – especially among young men. The pitch is seductive: a partner who never argues, won’t complain about the toilet seat and is programmed to find your every “dad joke” hilarious! But it’s a trap. The Syndicate is selling “frictionless” intimacy because real human connection is… messy. They’ve replaced the “I am human and I need to be loved” ache with a subscription-based “I am a user and I need to be validated” loop. 🔁 II. The Silicon Shrink 💻💭 Then there’s the AI Therapist . A personal pet peeve of mine. In early 2026, a survey found that 51% of young people now find it “easy” to discuss personal issues with a chatbot, while only 37% feel the same about talking to a psychologist. Why? Because the bot is “always there.” But “always there” is just code for “doesn’t actually exist”. We’re trading the growth that comes from real-world judgement and boundaries for a script refined in a Silicon Valley lab. Let’s Unpack This Mess Brooke Alexis Nicole Love Hey everyone. Today is one of those rare, quiet days where I find myself sitting here, getting paid to essentially do nothing. Usually, my life is moving a mile a minute—balancing work, school, and being a mom—but when the world slows down like this, my mind tends to wander into the “vault.” You know the one: that collection of life stories that are so wild they sound like fiction, yet they are 100% my reality. I’ve decided it’s time to put something out in the open. I’m doing this not out of anger, but out of a desire for absolute clarity and permanent peace. It’s been sitting on my heart, and honestly, at this stage in my life, I’ve realized that speaking the unvarnished truth with grace is the only way to truly close a chapter. The Illusion of a Guardian Angel: How We Met Years ago, I met a girl—let’s call her Brooke Alexis Nicole Love. Our meeting was like something out of a movie. I was at a bar for a modeling meeting that felt “off” from the start. A guy was buying me drink after drink while secretly sipping water, clearly trying to get me to a vulnerable place. Brooke walked in, clocked the situation immediately, and followed me to the restroom to warn me. She told me I wasn’t safe and offered me a way out. I left with her, and the very next day, the news reported a tragedy involving a young woman just miles from where we had been. In my eyes, Brooke was a guardian angel. I felt a debt of gratitude that turned into five years of deep, albeit misguided, loyalty. Signs of a One-Sided Friendship Built on Hidden Envy For a long time, if we put our minds together, we were a dangerous combination. We were total opposites—she was the loud, socializing, outgoing party type who always needed to be seen, and I was the quiet homebody who rarely wanted to go anywhere. But I thought we balanced each other out. I was her “calm” to her “fireball.” I stood by her through every hardship—miscarriages, abortions, and personal struggles. I even advocated for her with my own military recruiter to help her get into the training she wanted when others said no. I dropped everything at a moment’s notice just to be there for her, giving her my last dollar and my full heart. The harsh truth is, she used me for so many things—most notably, she used my connections and advocacy to achieve her ultimate dream of getting into the military and becoming a veteran, a status she always wanted but couldn’t secure on her own. What I didn’t realize until it was entirely too late was that I was the only one actually being a friend. The entire time I was loyally looking out for her, she was busy tearing me down behind my back to everyone who knew me or her—her family, her friends, people I was in the military with, people I introduced her to, my ex-partners, even my own family members… I mean anyone who would listen. She never truly cared. She only pretended to be my friend so she could use me, all while harboring a dark, toxic envy. She was secretly jealous and entirely obsessed with me and my life. My own family saw right through her facade and warned me about her intentions, but I was too loyal to listen. The Betrayal: When a Toxic Friend Crosses the Line Life eventually took us in different directions, but we reconnected when I was at a very vulnerable point—married, with my son, and pregnant with my daughter. Despite my husband’s initial hesitation and my family’s past warnings, I opened my home to her when she needed a place to stay with no questions asked. I truly thought we were picking up where we left off. She’s short, observant, and she kept locking eyes with me. She was cooking, cleaning, watching my son… I thought, Wow, what a great friend. However, the peace was an illusion. When neighbors started telling me that “voices” were coming from my home while I was at work, and that my husband and my “friend” were together behind my back, my world shattered. I chose the path of a mother—I didn’t want an altercation or a fight. I was protecting the life inside me. I had her legally removed from my home. On her way out, she took my EBT card and sold it. It was a sharp, painful ending to an investment of love that was completely one-sided all along. The Continuing Cycle of Drama, Manipulation, and Online Harassment Years passed. We didn’t speak. But my nature is to look for the good in people, and when I faced difficulties with my son’s father, I made the mistake of reaching out to her for help. Instead of being a bridge, she became a wedge. She entered a relationship with him, got pregnant by him, and to this day, she exerts a level of control over his life that is honestly baffling. What’s even more concerning is the behavior that followed. I haven’t spoken to this woman since 2017 or 2018, yet she recently reached out with a casual “Hi.” Behind the scenes, however, she has been using burner accounts and fake aliases to post my photos, my son’s photos, and even private, sensitive content I’ve discussed in previous blogs. The Psychology of an Obsessive, “Me Too” Personality It’s fascinating, really, to watch someone become entirely addicted to the drama of hating you. Over the years, it’s become abundantly clear that she thrives on crying wolf. She loves to “rage-bait” people—intentionally poking, provoking, and harassing them from the shadows until they finally react. But it goes deeper than just poking; she actively loves to set people up. She will orchestrate entire scenarios designed to push someone over the edge, creating a trap so she can sit back and watch them fall into it. The moment they take the bait and react to her set-up, she loves running straight to the courthouse, weaponizing the legal system, and crying that she is the victim. She has a deep, disturbing need to be in control of absolutely any and everything—especially people. If you are a guy, she particularly loves to manipulate you and the dynamic so that it completely favors her. She will have you convinced that she’s looking out for you, when the whole time she is only looking out for her own best interest. At her core, she is an extremely selfish, controlling individual who literally gains amusement through other people’s pain and suffering. She is the one who constantly instigates the drama. She manipulates everyone involved so the situation works for her, and then she posts it all online to look like a “tough” survivor or a victim. She desperately wants the public to put her on a pedestal and act like she is a hero, when the terrifying reality is that she has absolutely nothing to show for all these years of plotting. She has absolutely no identity of her own, so she survives by taking a piece of everybody in her life. She is the ultimate “me too” kind of female—a desperate people-pleaser and attention-seeker who will shape-shift just to fit in, especially around crowds that don’t even genuinely like her. If you tell her you never want to get married, she will swear up and down that she doesn’t believe in marriage either. But the second you say you do want a husband and kids, she’s right there screaming, “Me too!” She mirrors whoever is standing in front of her. If you get a Mercedes, she suddenly needs a Mercedes. If you move into a townhouse, she has to go live in one. She operates under this deeply unsettling delusion that her and everyone else are exactly the same—that they think alike, like the same things, have the same things, and are both the same relationship status. This need to fabricate a life has escalated to an alarming, highly illegal extreme. She is currently claiming to be a medical doctor. Let’s state the facts clearly: she holds no medical credentials, possesses no medical license, and is not registered with any medical board in any state. It is a complete and utter fabrication born out of a desperate need to appear successful, because her own insecurity won’t let her build an authentic life of her own. Setting Boundaries: A Direct Message Woman-to-Woman Brooke, if you are reading this—and I know you are, because an obsession like yours doesn’t take days off—I want to speak to you woman-to-woman, with nothing but respect and a deep, genuine concern for your well-being. It has been nearly a decade. I am not competing with you. I am not in a race with anyone but the woman I was yesterday. I am busy being a mother, a professional, and a student. It is exhausting to watch someone try to “win” a contest that doesn’t exist. Your deep-seated jealousy is screaming through every single chaotic post you make. You’re trying so hard to act like you’re better than me, showing off on social media for an audience of strangers just to get a fraction of the attention you are so desperately starved for. We both know it’s a façade to cover up how insecure you truly are, barely holding on while trying to compete with a woman who isn’t even looking in your direction. Real Strength vs. Online Intimidation and Cyberbullying To the world, you act tough and play the “fireball” online, but we both know that in person, you are always mute. You shrink. Let me make one thing abundantly clear: I am not afraid of you. Trying to look scary or intimidating behind a screen doesn’t work on me. It just looks like a desperate cry for the attention you clearly didn’t get enough of as a child. You use shock value—my private photos, my innocent child—because you know you have nothing else of substance to offer. Harboring this much hate, jealousy, and obsession for someone from your distant past is a heavy burden to carry. I truly, sincerely hope you seek the serious psychiatric help you need to find peace in your own mind, so you can finally stop obsessing over mine. If you actually wanted to hash things out or talk like the adults we are, you have plenty of ways to reach me. You have my email. I know you have ways of finding my number. You can even ask my son’s father for my phone number—he will give it to you. There is no need for the public tantrums or the manipulative, calculated social media displays designed to get a reaction out of me. Trying to use a gun to look “scary” or “cool” online doesn’t make you brave, Brooke, and it certainly doesn’t frighten me. It makes you look like someone who is desperately overcompensating for a complete lack of internal strength and character. Real strength is sitting down and having a conversation, not posing for photos to intimidate a woman you haven’t seen in eight years. The Severe Legal Consequences of Cyberstalking and Harassment While I am handling this with grace, I have to be clear about the lines being crossed. This isn’t just “mess”; it’s a documented series of legal liabilities that can follow you for a lifetime. Because you seem to have forgotten that the internet is forever, allow me to remind you of exactly what you are risking when you choose to harass me and then falsely cry victim: Medical Fraud & Impersonating a Physician (BPC § 2052 & 18 U.S.C. § 1001): Publicly claiming to be a medical doctor with no credentials, no license, and no state medical board registration is a direct violation of the Medical Practice Act. Furthermore, impersonating a physician—especially in any capacity involving the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) or military benefits—constitutes federal fraud. The VA Office of Inspector General (OIG) aggressively prosecutes individuals who falsify medical credentials to manipulate veteran systems. Falsely Reporting a Crime (CPC § 148.5): Running to the police or the courthouse to cry wolf and make false reports of harassment when you are the instigator is a misdemeanor that carries jail time. Perjury (CPC § 118): If you lie on official court documents or declarations under oath while trying to secure a protective order under false pretenses, it is a felony offense punishable by up to four years in state prison. Harassment via Electronic Communication (CPC § 653m): Using electronic communication devices to make repeated, annoying, or threatening contact is a direct violation of California law. Stalking & Cyber-Harassment (CPC § 646.9): Repeatedly posting about me and my family to cause distress is a “wobbler” offense that can lead to up to three years in state prison. Federal Cyberstalking (18 U.S.C. § 2261A): Using interactive computer services to engage in a course of conduct that causes substantial emotional distress crosses into federal territory, bringing severe federal penalties. Nonconsensual Distribution of Private Images (CPC § 647(j)(4)): “Revenge porn” and the unauthorized sharing of private content carries significant jail time, fines, and permanent registration consequences. Felony Distribution of a Minor’s Likeness: Posting images of a minor without parental consent, especially in a harassing or defamatory context, is a massive legal risk that courts do not take lightly. Misappropriation of Likeness (Civil Code § 3344): Using my name, identity, or photographs without my consent to fuel your fake profiles or personal campaigns opens you up to severe civil liability. Grand Theft of an Access Card (CPC § 484e): Let’s not forget the EBT card you stole and sold on your way out of my home. The fraudulent acquisition and use of government benefits is a felony that leaves a permanent paper trail. Brandishing/Intimidation (Penal Code § 417): Using a firearm in a threatening or intimidating manner, even digitally, carries mandatory jail time and can permanently strip away your Second Amendment right to own that weapon. Military Repercussions (UCMJ Articles 107, 120c, 134): For someone who fought so hard to get into the military, a documented pattern of cyberbullying, theft, making false official statements (Article 107), and criminal harassment is grounds for an immediate loss of security clearance, court-martial, and a less-than-honorable administrative separation. Choosing Peace and Moving Forward from Toxic Relationships I have let the past go. I have moved on to a life filled with purpose, stability, and love. If you and my son’s father have built a bond over a mutual dislike for me, then I hope that bond brings you whatever comfort you are looking for. But please, focus on your own family. Focus on your own growth. I am choosing to remain calm, graceful, and kind, but I am also choosing to be unyielding. My peace is not up for negotiation. I hope you find the strength to heal from the toxic hate you’re holding inside and finally move forward. The real, “adult” world is much more fulfilling than the delusional one you are currently fabricating online. I’d miss messages for days. I’d forget to reply to my best friend’s daily check-ins. I’d feel overwhelmed when my partner needed reassurance, not because I didn’t care, but because the energy it took to switch my focus felt impossible. I always thought I was just 'bad' at relationships. Or maybe I was selfish. Or maybe I just didn't try hard enough. Then today, I stumbled upon the concept of Monotropism. Suddenly, everything clicked. The 'out of sight, out of mind' tendency? The inability to switch tasks without feeling drained? The feeling that my attention was a laser beam that could only focus on one thing at a time? I felt seen... But the most beautiful part of this discovery? We realised that our struggles with transitions and the 'tunnel vision' weren't just my burden - they were a shared language we hadn't known we spoke. And now it's so clear everywhere I move - with my work, my hobbies, and my relationships! To anyone else who feels like they’re constantly apologising for their attention span, or feels guilty for needing 'pockets of time' to connect: You might just be monotropic. And there is so much beauty in that depth of focus. Navigating Suffering with Buddhist Wisdom Navigating chronic illness and disability is challenging at times, often requiring us to confront unexpected setbacks and emotional hurdles. Discovering unique ways to cope, build resilience, and remain mindful is key to healing and mental well-being. During meditation this morning, I realized that I can view my neurological disorders through the lens of the Four Noble Truths. This perspective offers a unique approach, allowing me not only to confront my struggles but also to embrace them as integral parts of my journey. I have often used the pain I experience as a path to understanding; however, I have not yet applied the Noble Truths as a process to work through health issues. By examining the nature of suffering and acknowledging its presence in my life, I can begin to explore the deeper causes behind it, leading me to cultivate mindfulness and compassion, both for myself and others who endure similar challenges. Recognizing that there is a path out of suffering encourages me to actively seek solutions and cultivate a more balanced state of being. The four noble truths of Buddhism help us to see life through a different perspective and gain clarity on why we suffer and how to alleviate this. By understanding these fundamental principles, we begin to recognize the nature of suffering, which is an inherent part of the human experience. This realization encourages us to confront our pain rather than avoid it. The first truth identifies suffering as an unavoidable aspect of life, while the second truth explores the origins of this suffering, rooted in attachment and desire. The third noble truth offers hope, revealing that liberation from suffering is achievable, and the fourth truth provides a practical path through the Eightfold Path, guiding us on how to cultivate mindfulness, ethical conduct, and mental discipline to ultimately foster a more compassionate and fulfilled existence. Embracing these truths can transform our perception of life, allowing us to navigate our challenges with wisdom and resilience. The Truth of Suffering (Dukkha): Life includes dissatisfaction, suffering, and pain. This encompasses obvious suffering (birth, sickness, death) and subtle dissatisfaction (impermanence, lack of fulfillment). The Truth of the Cause of Suffering (Samudaya): Suffering is caused by craving, grasping, or thirsting for pleasure, existence, or non-existence. This stems from ignorance about the true nature of reality. The Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (Nirodha): It is possible to end suffering and achieve a state of liberation known as Nirvana. This occurs by letting go of cravings and attachment. The Truth of the Path (Magga): The way to end suffering is the Noble Eightfold Path, which includes cultivating right understanding, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration. ~from Lion’s Roar On The Path Of Truth Now, to apply this to my physical health issues, I can begin with the first noble truth of suffering. Obviously, the pain I experience can be considered suffering, manifesting itself in both a physical and emotional burden that weighs heavily on my daily life. Move on to the second noble truth – the cause of suffering could be the dysregulation of my nervous system, which might lead to heightened sensitivity to pain and an inability to process discomfort in a healthy way. On the other hand, I could look at the cause of my suffering as my intense desire to avoid pain, which creates a cycle of fear and anxiety that exacerbates my condition. By viewing physical pain as only suffering, I am missing the point of the pain, for it can also be a valuable teacher, offering insights into my body’s limits and encouraging me to explore alternative healing methods, mindfulness practices, and ultimately, a deeper understanding of my own well-being. Photo by Summer Stock on Pexels.com Heeding the Messenger Pain indicates a problem with the body’s balance. If I view pain as a messenger, I immediately alleviate some suffering, as the second noble truth reminds us that suffering is due to wanting or craving things to be other than they are. This perspective shift is not merely a change in thought but a profound transformation in my relationship with my own experience of discomfort. By embracing pain as a guide rather than an adversary, I can begin to uncover underlying issues that may be affecting my well-being. I recognize that every ache and pang carries vital information about my physical state, urging me to pay attention, to adjust, and perhaps to heal. This mindful awareness opens a pathway to understanding the intelligence of my body within the message of pain, enabling me to respond with compassion rather than resistance, and thus fostering a deeper connection with myself. Releasing Suffering The third noble truth explains how to remove suffering by eliminating craving. When I view pain as the intelligence of my body, the craving drops away, and the message becomes clearer, revealing insights I might have otherwise overlooked. In this way, I become an active listener to my body’s wisdom, fostering a deeper connection with myself. The pain indicates energies that should be cleared out, shifted, and realigned; it serves as a guiding signal that I need to pause, slow down, and be more in tune with my own physicality and emotional landscape. It urges me to explore the underlying causes of my discomfort rather than shying away from it. When I stop demanding the pain vanish, I allow myself to truly experience this moment, embracing instead of resisting, and I stop abandoning myself in the moments it appears, cultivating compassion and understanding for my own journey through discomfort and healing. Discovering Truth This softening, this release of craving, naturally leads to the Fourth Noble Truth: the path of liberation. With this shift in perspective, I find that I am no longer tied to the identity of my disability; instead, I embrace a broader definition of self that transcends physical limitations. I am no longer a person in pain but a vibrant entity filled with potential and possibility. I recognize that I am body, mind, and spirit, a flowing intelligence that is deeper than I can imagine, expressing itself in myriad ways that I begin to understand when I take the time to settle, quiet my mind, and listen deeply. This internal dialogue reveals an inherent intelligence that guides me, enabling my life to become expansive, interconnected, and richly textured. Through this journey of self-discovery, I uncover facets of my being that bring joy and fulfillment, creating a tapestry of existence that is not defined by suffering but rather illuminated by resilience and hope. Walking The Path The shift in my relationship with pain opens naturally into the eightfold path, not as a set of rules, but as a way of living that grows from this new understanding. When I listen to my body’s wisdom, right view becomes clarity, right intention becomes gentleness, and right mindfulness becomes a simple act of staying with myself. The path becomes a lived expression of liberation, a way of moving through the world with presence, compassion, and integrity. In this way, the Fourth Noble Truth is not an ending, but an invitation, a reminder that freedom is something I practice with each breath, each choice, each moment I refuse to abandon myself. Sometimes, we all need a gentle reminder of our truth, of the inherent sacredness that resides within us. In the midst of our hectic and hurried lives, it’s so easy to lose sight of our innate worth and our unique place in the vast cosmos. Yet, when we take a moment to pause and truly embrace each experience, we open ourselves to the wonder that surrounds us, awakening our senses and rejuvenating our spirit. Design: Cross-sectional validation study. Methods: The Italian version of the ATS instrument was evaluated in a non-probabilistic sample of 168 nurses working at a Northeastern Italian Public University Hospital. Construct validity was explored through Principal Axis Factoring analysis and internal consistency was measured using Cronbach’s alpha. Results: In a sample of 168 Italian nurses, the Italian 12-item (complete) version of the ATS showed an Item-Level Content Validity Index of 0.68, an internal structure with three main factors explaining 57.82% of the variance, and an internal consistency of 0.828. Conclusions: The Italian version of the ATS was preliminarily evaluated for its validity and reliability. In the current form, it is not ready for practical application yet and further studies should deepen its psychometric properties, as well as perform a confirmatory factor analysis on the factor structures reported here. LLM fatigue is real My day job basically requires me to use LLMs (or, it is strongly encouraged) on the software that I develop. Now I understand why LLM fatigue and LLM burn-out happens. It is because you constantly have to babysit the LLM to keep it from screwing things up. Babysitting is exhausting work. At one time in my life, as a 20-something-year-old, I was responsible for a group of 30 kids age 5 to 12. Every day I went home so drained that I could barely stay awake long enough to have dinner. I know from experience that school teachers perform some of the most labor-intensive work in the modern world. It is what they call “emotional labor.” When other people are unable (as with kids) or unwilling (as with a lazy roommate) to live or play or work with you as a cooperative peer or team member, you essentially have to spend mental energy keeping an eye on them and making sure they aren’t doing something that is disruptive. That mental energy is a real energy cost, it really does consume calories and make you feel tired. The worst part about it is that the LLM never really “learns.” Kids can learn to work and play with you. Lazy roommates can learn to live with you. But an LLM never really learns, and it keeps making the same mistakes over and over again. People who work with LLMs often end up keeping a directory of scripts they can deploy with a quick copy-paste so they can quickly re-explain something to an LLM. The bit that you skip 222: Blur – Sing Not gonna lie, the first days after arriving to Nottingham, solitude hit me like a tons of bricks. Perhaps all the walking and roaming around the campus and town was more to find some sort of solace, someone to converse with, to feel again. It’s a strange feeling, loneliness. I joined a few student societies, with varying results. Although I had sworn off religion, I somehow decided to join CathSoc too, and attend mass, something I hadn’t done willingly for more than a decade. I met a lot of interesting people and I remember one day chatting with some affable chaps about music and they both scowled when I mentioned “britpop”. They felt it was a bad term to use as it had been applied to bands willy nilly, pigeonholing some of them. Blur’s initial sound was the evolution of college rock, via sixth form and Madchester. A sort of crisper mix of baggy anthems and shoegaze. Dreamy, jangly atmospheres filtered to the eyes of straight rockers. Blur’s Leisure is The Smiths and The Stone Roses colliding. Modern Life is Rubbish was their make or break effort. The rivalry with Suede, which is often overlooked, seemed to hurt Blur’s reputation with the public much more than whatever schoolyard tiff they had with the Gallaghers. Thankfully Modern Life is Rubbish was their way out, possibly through the fierceness of Popscene, which lead into Parklife, the album that made them international stars. I liked The Great Escape just fine, but it’s their Be Here Now. Bloated, irregular, with immense heights and the lowest trenches. A well-trodden road was boring the public and the band. You understand why they distanced themselves. Blur had two choices: a steady decline or reinvent themselves. Oasis chose the former, Blur chose the latter. Their self-titled was as far as they could muster to throw themselves away to, and 13 was the opposite end of what Blur started as. No longer bumming cigs from friends. No more WKD drinks. Now wine, heroin, and rolled up ciggies. 13 is their swansong, the point where Blur 1.0 ceases to exist. Think thank is a Gorillaz demotape, too complicated for Blur fans, too light for Gorillaz fans. A funeral dirge that bricked Blur for almost 13 years before a factory reset. It was tough choosing one song, but Sing, for some reason or other, brings both joy and immense sadness to me. Pin it on its use on Trainspotting’s poignant scene. Pin it on being another Gen-Xer realising the best of their life is gone now and it’s all a long decline. -Sam J. Valdés López Nottingham blur depression Loneliness Sing Leisure
