The Closed Door Trilogy: Part Two: The Bottom You Know When You Are There There is no dramatic announcement. No moment where the floor gives way and you fall through into something recognizably worse. The bottom just arrives. You realize you have been there for a few days already and did not mark the entry point. You look around at the interior of whatever this place is and understand, with a clarity that is almost clinical, that this is as far down as it goes. For him it looked like three days without leaving the apartment. It looked like food ordered because eating felt necessary and not because hunger had made itself known. It looked like the phone face-down on the table and the table existing at the far end of a room that felt very large. The Silence Gets Loud At the bottom, the silence stops being neutral. It accumulates. He could hear it in the way you hear a frequency that was always there but only becomes audible when everything else is gone. The absence of other people, of obligation, of performance, left him alone with a version of himself he did not particularly want to spend extended time with. He tried music once. Turned it off after four minutes. The gap between how it sounded and how he felt was too wide and the contrast made things worse. He tried television. Watched forty minutes of something he cannot now remember and turned it off because the people on screen seemed to be operating in a different physical reality, one where faces moved and mouths made sounds for reasons that felt alien and exhausting to track. What Nobody Sees Outside the door, life continued at its regular pace. He knew this in the abstract. People were having lunch and making plans and sending messages he was not answering and probably, some of them, wondering if they had done something wrong. He felt bad about that in the part of himself that was still capable of feeling bad about things. The part had gotten smaller. He cried once, on the second day. Not with any particular trigger. Just the accumulated pressure of everything finding its only available exit. He sat on the bathroom floor because that is where it happened, and he let it run its course, and then he washed his face with cold water and looked at himself in the mirror for a long time without thinking anything in particular, and then he went back to the room and the silence and the phone face-down on the table. The Knock on the Third Day He did not answer it. But he heard it. And then he heard a voice through the door, not asking to be let in, not demanding an explanation, just saying his name and then saying: I am going to leave something here. You do not have to open the door. I just wanted you to know I came. He sat very still on the other side of the door and listened to the footsteps move away down the hall. He did not open the door for another hour. When he did, there was food and a note that said nothing except: still here when you are ready. He stood in the doorway and looked at the empty hallway for a long time. He did not feel better. But he felt something shift, some small tectonic thing deep underneath the weight, that was not better exactly but was different from what it had been five minutes before. The Bottom Is Not the End That is what he learned on the third day, not as an insight or a revelation, just as a fact he had gathered enough evidence to provisionally accept. The bottom has a floor. It is not bottomless. You hit it and it holds you, not comfortably, not warmly, but structurally. It does not let you through. He ate the food. He read the note twice. He did not text back that night. But he kept the note. fictionSeries healingAlone Loneliness mentalHealth shortStorySeries silentSuffering socialMedia theClosedDoorTrilogy ZsoltZsemba

The Closed Door Trilogy: Part One: The Descent It Starts Before You Notice It Starting It never arrives all at once. That is the thing nobody tells you. It does not show up at the door with its name on a sign. It seeps in. A Tuesday that feels heavier than it should. A conversation that leaves you emptier than before it happened. A moment where you look at the life around you and feel nothing that resembles ownership of it. You notice you have stopped laughing at things that used to be funny. You notice the bed feels like the only honest place in the room. By the time you realize what is happening, it has already been happening for a while. The Door Closes Quietly He did not make a decision to pull back. It just happened the way erosion happens. Gradually, then completely. First, he stopped returning calls he would have returned before. Then he started leaving messages on read without the guilt that used to follow. Then the invitations stopped feeling like opportunities and started feeling like obligations he did not have the resources to meet. He told himself it was temporary. He told himself he just needed a few days to reset, to find his footing, to get back to some version of himself that felt inhabitable. He believed it the first few times he said it. By the third week, he had stopped keeping count. What the Darkness Actually Feels Like People use darkness as a metaphor, and it is not wrong, but it is incomplete. It is not just the absence of light. It is the presence of weight. Everything costs more than it should. Getting up costs something. Eating costs something. Responding to a simple question from someone who genuinely cares costs something he does not always have on hand. He moves through the hours like a man walking against a current that nobody else in the room can feel. He does not talk about it. Not because there are no words. There are too many words, and none of them land anywhere useful. He has tried before. He has watched the face of someone listening arrange itself into concern and felt the distance between what he was trying to say and what they were able to receive, and decided the gap was not worth crossing. The Worst Nights Have a Particular Quality They are quieter than the others. Not peaceful and quiet. The kind of quiet that has texture. He lies in the dark, and the thoughts are not dramatic, which somehow makes them worse. They are just steady and low and certain in the way that exhausted things are certain. He does not spiral. He just sinks. Slowly, without theatrics, into something he cannot quite name but recognizes by now. He knows people are out there. He can picture them, specific faces, people who would pick up on the first ring. He does not reach for the phone. Not because he does not want a connection. Because want requires energy, he is running too low to access. He Will Not Tell You How Close It Gets Not tonight. Maybe not ever. There are edges in those nights that he does not revisit in daylight, not because they were not real, but because bringing them back into the light feels like giving them more oxygen than they deserve. What he will tell you is that the night always ends. Not cleanly. Not with resolution. Just with the particular gray that comes before morning, the colour of something that has not decided yet what it is going to be. He makes it to the gray every time. He has not yet decided if that is a strength or just the stubbornness of a body that keeps going before the mind has agreed to. Either way, he is still here at the start of the next day. Still behind the door. Still in the dark. fictionSeries healingAlone Loneliness shortStorySeries silentSuffering theClosedDoorTrilogy ZsoltZsemba

Thousands of Followers and Nearly Completely Alone? We Built the Most Connected World in History and Somehow Got Lonelier Somewhere between the first social media account and the ten thousandth follower, something shifted. Not dramatically. Not all at once. Just quietly, the way the most important changes tend to happen. We started measuring our social lives in metrics. Reach. Engagement. Impressions. We started performing connections instead of having it. And we got so good at the performance that most of us stopped noticing the difference. The numbers went up. The loneliness went up with them. That is not a coincidence. What the Research Actually Says The evidence on social media and mental health has been building for years, and it is not ambiguous. Studies consistently show that heavy social media use is associated with higher rates of anxiety, depression, and loneliness across all age groups, with the sharpest effects in adolescents and young adults. A 2023 report from the US Surgeon General identified social media as a significant contributing factor to the youth mental health crisis, noting that adolescents who spend more than three hours a day on social platforms face double the risk of depression and anxiety symptoms. The comparison effect is relentless. Every scroll is a highlight reel from someone else’s life positioned against the unedited reality of your own. The brain was not built to process that volume of social comparison. For most of human history, you compared yourself to maybe a few dozen people you actually knew. Now you compare yourself to thousands of curated strangers before breakfast. The AI Problem Nobody Is Talking About Loudly Enough And then there is AI. Tools like the one generating this post. Conversational, available around the clock, endlessly patient, never tired, never distracted, never having a bad day that bleeds into how it treats you. It is easy to see why people find that appealing. It is also worth being honest about what it costs. When you can have a conversation with an AI instead of texting a friend, you remove the friction of a human relationship. The vulnerability. The reciprocity. The fact that the other person has their own needs, bad days and limits. That friction is not a flaw in human connection. It is the mechanism by which genuine intimacy is built. Remove it, and you get something that feels like connection but does not do what connection actually does for a human nervous system. AI does not replace human connection. It displaces the impulse to seek it. And that is a different and more subtle kind of damage. Thousands of Followers and a Silent Phone There is a specific kind of loneliness that belongs to the social media age, and it does not have a clean name yet. It is the loneliness of someone whose content reaches ten thousand people and who has nobody to call when something goes wrong. The loneliness of being publicly visible and privately invisible. The loneliness of a comment section full of strangers and a contact list full of people you have not spoken to in months because the algorithm convinced you that posting was the same as connecting. It is not. Posting is broadcasting. Connection requires two people actually showing up for each other, imperfectly, in real time, with something genuinely at stake. The Mental Health Crisis Nobody Wants to Fully Acknowledge Rates of depression, anxiety, and suicide have climbed steadily in the years since smartphones became ubiquitous. The World Health Organization estimates that more than 700,000 people die by suicide each year globally, making it one of the leading causes of death among people aged 15 to 29. That number existed before social media. But the platforms have added new dimensions to the problem: cyberbullying, social exclusion that happens publicly and permanently, the pressure to perform wellness while privately deteriorating, and the algorithmic amplification of content that keeps distressed people in loops of distressing material. The person posting daily about their perfect life may be falling apart privately. The person who has gone quiet on their feed may be going dark in the way that actually matters. The metrics tell you nothing about what is actually happening inside the person generating them. What to Do If You Are the Person Behind the Closed Door If any of this is landing somewhere personal, that matters more than anything else in this post. The research on social isolation and mental health is clear: connection with other humans, a real connection, is one of the most protective factors against depression and suicidal thinking. Not followers. Not likes. Not an AI that is available at 3 am. Actual people who know you and show up. If you are struggling and not reaching out because you do not want to be a burden, consider this: the people who care about you would rather be burdened than uninformed. And if there is nobody in your immediate life you feel you can reach, there are people whose entire purpose is to be there for exactly that moment. Indonesia: Into The Light at 119 International: The International Association for Suicide Prevention maintains a directory of crisis centers at Global: The WHO mental health resources are available at The Algorithm Is Not Your Friend. But You Probably Have Some. Log off for an hour. Text someone you have not spoken to in a while. Have a conversation that cannot be liked, shared or measured in any way. Let it be awkward, imperfect, and human. That is not a step backward from modern life. It is the thing modern life keeps trying to replace with something that looks similar but does not actually work. You have followers. Go find your people. Marriage Won’t Fix Your Loneliness There’s a version of loneliness that nobody talks about honestly. Not the kind that hits you on a Friday night when your phone isn’t buzzing. The deeper kind. The kind that follows you into a full house, a shared bed, a family dinner table. The kind that makes you wonder why, with all these people around, you still feel completely alone. Most men don’t sit with that question long enough to answer it. They solve it instead. They find a woman, build something with her, have kids, chase a bigger salary, fill the calendar. For a while, it works, or it feels like it works. Then one day the noise dies down, and there it is again. Same heaviness. Same hollow feeling. Waiting. That’s because loneliness isn’t a situation. It’s a symptom. What You’re Actually Running From The problem isn’t that you’re single, or broke, or sexually frustrated. Those things might be true, and they’re worth addressing on their own terms. But the loneliness underneath all of that isn’t going away because your circumstances improved. It goes away when you look at what’s actually driving it. For most men, that loneliness traces back to something specific. A version of themselves they abandoned at some point. The kid who was told to stop being so sensitive. The teenager who learned that vulnerability gets punished. The adult who built walls so convincing that he forgot they were walls. He walks through life making connections without actually making them. He builds a family and realizes he doesn’t know how to let them in. Marriage doesn’t fix that. It exposes it. Why the Big Moves Don’t Work There’s a reason so many men arrive at forty with everything they thought they wanted and still feel like something is missing. The house, the kids, the career, the relationship. All checked. And yet. The problem is the logic of acquisition. We are raised to believe that the right external circumstances will produce the right internal state. Get the girl, feel worthy. Make the money, feel secure. Start a family, feel complete. This is how most men operate for the better part of their lives, and it produces results that look great in photos and feel hollow in private. Sex doesn’t fix loneliness either. It can mask it for an hour. A good night with someone you care about can make you feel close, connected, and seen. But if you’re using sex to feel less alone, you already know how fast that wears off. You already know the feeling of lying next to someone and still being completely inside your own head. None of these things is wrong to want. The problem is expecting them to do a job they were never designed to do. The Only Thing That Actually Works Coming to terms with your issues is not a therapy cliche. It’s the unsexy, uncomfortable, non-negotiable work of actually understanding yourself. Why do you respond the way you do? What you’re afraid of. What you’ve been carrying since before you had the language for it. What you keep recreating in every relationship because you never dealt with it the first time. This is where most men tap out. It’s easier to find a new woman than to face why the last three relationships followed the same pattern. Easier to work longer hours than to sit with the discomfort of not knowing who you are outside of productivity. Easier to have another drink, plan another trip, start another project. The men who do the work stop feeling as lonely. Not because their circumstances became perfect, but because they stopped being strangers to themselves. When you actually know who you are, a real connection becomes possible. Not the performance of it. This Isn’t About Going It Alone None of this means marriage is pointless or that kids won’t add something real to your life. It means the sequence matters. If you bring an unexamined version of yourself into a relationship, you bring your unresolved loneliness with you. The other person becomes responsible for fixing something they didn’t break and can’t reach. The men who build something genuinely good with another person tend to be the ones who have spent real time understanding themselves first. Not perfectly. Not with every issue resolved. But with enough self-awareness to stop outsourcing their emotional life to whoever is standing closest. You can get married. You can have kids. You can make a lot of money and have a very active sex life. All of that is available to you. But if you skip the part where you actually deal with yourself, you will feel alone in every single one of those situations. That’s not a warning. It’s just what happens. alone emptiness familyAndFriends friends frustrated Loneliness marriage partners ZsoltZsemba

If You Don’t Know Who You Are Alone, Relationships Will Confuse the Hell Out of You Nobody tells you this when you’re young. You spend your whole adolescence being shaped by what other people think of you, what your parents wanted you to become, and what the culture tells you success looks like. You absorb all of it. You build a personality around it. And then one day you find yourself in a relationship, wondering why you feel so lost, why you keep reacting in ways you don’t fully understand, why the person across from you seems to trigger something you can’t quite name. The answer is usually the same. You never figured out who you are when nobody is watching. Most men walk into relationships as a work in progress; they haven’t started yet. They know their job title, their taste in music, and their football team. They don’t know their patterns. They don’t know what they actually need versus what they think they’re supposed to want. They don’t know where they end, and other people begin. So when a relationship puts pressure on all of that, the confusion is total. The Mirror Problem Relationships have a way of reflecting things back at you. A partner who pulls away makes you realize you have an abandonment wound you never addressed. A partner who criticizes you activates something from childhood you thought you’d outgrown. A partner who needs too much space makes you question your own worth in ways that have nothing to do with them. None of this is their fault. The mirror doesn’t create what it shows you. It just shows you. The problem is that most men haven’t done the work to understand what they’re looking at when it appears. So instead of recognizing the reflection, they blame the mirror. They blame her for being distant, critical, or suffocating. They end the relationship. They find a new one. The same patterns show up again within six months, wearing a different face. This is not bad luck. This is what happens when you enter a relationship without knowing yourself. What You Think You Want vs. What You Actually Need Here’s where it gets complicated. A man who doesn’t know himself doesn’t know the difference between what he wants and what he needs. He thinks he wants a woman who doesn’t challenge him. What he needs is someone who makes him feel safe enough to be honest. He thinks he wants constant closeness. What he needs is to learn that he can be alone without falling apart. He thinks he wants someone to fix the emptiness. What he needs is to stop outsourcing that job. This gap between want and need is where most relationships quietly die. Two people who both don’t know themselves, trying to fill in the blanks with each other, eventually realizing the blanks are still there and blaming each other for it. You cannot bridge that gap from inside a relationship. You can do some of the work there, if you’re lucky and both people are willing. But the foundation has to be laid before you walk in. Alone Is the Practice Ground Being alone is not a waiting room. It’s not the unpleasant gap between relationships that you have to survive until the next one starts. It’s the only place where you can actually hear yourself think without someone else’s needs, expectations, or projections filling up the space. When you’re alone, and you sit with that discomfort instead of immediately solving it, you learn something. You learn what actually bothers you versus what you can let go. You learn how you talk to yourself when nobody is listening. You learn whether you actually like your own company, and if you don’t, that tells you something important. The men who figure out who they are when they’re alone tend to show up differently in relationships. Not perfectly. Not without issues. But with enough self-knowledge to stop reacting blindly, to take some responsibility for their patterns, to ask for what they need instead of punishing a partner for not reading their mind. The Real Cost of Skipping This Skipping the work of knowing yourself doesn’t just hurt you. It hurts whoever you’re with. You become unpredictable to them because you’re unpredictable to yourself. You make them responsible for your emotional stability. You confuse love with need and then resent them when they can’t meet all of it. The relationships that actually work, the ones that hold up under pressure and still feel like something good years later, are almost always built by people who came in with some degree of self-knowledge. Not perfect self-knowledge. Just enough to know where they were standing. You can start a relationship without knowing yourself. Plenty of people do. But at some point, the confusion becomes impossible to ignore. The question is whether you address it before it costs you something you actually care about. Does the male loneliness epidemic really exist? Throughout history, even in the beliefs they fabricated, men found a way to unite. They supported each other or challenged each other, somehow remaining connected. They clinked glasses in pubs, or smashed bottles over each other's heads. They womanized together, committed crimes together, debated ideas, collectively pacified others (regardless of their gender), understood each other with just a glance. They flattered each other, shared their feelings in the limited ways they knew. They left their families to gamble in casinos, supported each other on the front lines of the wars they themselves started, formed brotherhood bonds with their army buddies, writing a magnificent history of brotherhood. Men were always together. They slept together, had sex with each other without anyone knowing, they fought each other and then made peace, like brothers who fought and then hugged in the playground, but never truly separated. Does this make masculinity a bit like the biggest single-cell organism in history? Or is there a collective delusion to deflect blame? Just pause for a second, And think. Maybe it's not loneliness. Maybe it's just the personal and painful realisation that one is simply an ordinary human being. "Why wasn't I declared the most special, the most powerful, the alpha, the king, as I hoped? Why wasn't I made to feel 'most privileged' by everyone? Why do I have to strive for money, education, status, sex? Why do I have to work hard for respect? Why isn't masculinity alone enough to make others carry me on their shoulders" Maybe penis is not a divine sceptre, no matter how much the world wants you to believe in that. I’ve spent most of the day in tears over it (5,299 words written today; this shows you how deeply I was in it). It is the original wound for Storymere (that takes you to more detail about the story’s concept; this takes you to another excerpt). This story is one I care very deeply about. I hope you come to love these characters as much as I do. Ultimately, the novel traces this family over the course of 100 years. I wake while it is still night. I know it’s too early to rise because the shape of Neene still lies on her mat, her body turned toward us. The room is grey and still and quiet except for Awa. She breathes with her mouth parted, as though she can’t be quiet even when she’s asleep. Something scratches outside. One of the village dogs or a curious goat looks for scraps. When I roll, I notice Baaba’s sleeping place is empty; his mat, rolled up neatly, leans against the woven wall. Frowning, I sit, yawning. There’s no sense in letting daylight waste away. Neene says this when she catches Awa sitting still instead of finding something useful to do. Neene would smile at me, pat my back, and tell me thank you if some of the chores are done before Fajr. I stand silently, smiling when a sliver of moonlight reveals a speck of dust on Awa’s chin. She just can’t help herself: dirt gathers around her like bees to honey. I hesitate but choose my pretty blue wrapper to wear. When I pull the nightshift off, gooseflesh rises along the thin, soft hairs of my legs. I haven’t worn the pretty blue wrapper since Neene and Baaba gave it to me; it still feels stiff as it drapes around me, its ends brushing lightly against my ankles. When I step outside, I look up first. The sky still holds the stars; they twinkle above me. Since I’ll have to wash my feet for Fajr anyway, I don’t wear my sandals. The gritty, tawny dirt beneath my soles feels like home. The thought makes me look beyond the hills toward the river and Samba’s settlement. “Do ya think that’s enoug’?” Sometimes his words curl around each other, the beginnings and endings blurring. “Do you think that’s enough for a hearth?” I ask as we stare into the small brown box where a handful of Djéol dirt now lies. “You add some.” Small pebbles and bits of loose rock and dirt harden the ground; a jagged crack formed by the dry season’s relentless sun snags the corner of my gaze. I work to loosen the dirt until it crumbles; using the side of one hand, I scoop some into my other palm. The whispering sound of it sliding into the box and onto the dirt he’s already collected sounds almost like a promise. Samba’s face changes; his smile grows. “That’s enough gold.” Feeding the poultry is Awa’s morning chore, but when I see the coarse-woven sack lying on its side, its mouth open and a light dusting of millet spilt onto the ground, I shake my head. She left the millet out and some animal got into it . A few tiny tracks near the sack confirm a mouse found an easy supper. Bending down, I scoop the excess millet into my palm and toss it over the pen for the chickens. Soon, I’ve cleaned the ground, fed them and returned the tied sack to storage. The mouse will have to look elsewhere for food tonight. The sound of a donkey braying turns my head. Baaba. The donkey’s ears twitch as he stops near the hut. Neene comes out, calls hello and walks toward the earthen wall. Baaba dismounts, checks the sky. Fajr nears. “Isn’t that your sister’s task?” he asks, his brows arched. I shrug. “There was time to do it now.” “Everything alright?” Neene asks, coming back, glancing at the horizon. Baaba nods. “Bocar and I went; we didn’t see anything around the boundary.” Taking the rope tied around the donkey’s neck, Baaba walks toward the tethering post. Neene’s shoulders loosen. “Good. I’ll start the water.” The air in the hut feels different when I step back inside; alive instead of asleep. Except for Awa. She still lies with her eyes closed and her mouth open, her breathing slow and steady. Reaching down, I shake her arm. She frowns, her lips closing, and rolls away from me. “Come on, Awa. It’s time for wudu and prayer.” I shake her again. When she doesn’t open her eyes, I coil my pinkie around a fuzzy curl and give two quick tugs. She moans, her hand reaching out to slap my arm. “Stop,” she moans. “Get up.” Her mouth stretches wide, yawning, and one honey-brown eye opens. I smile. “Good morning, Awa.” Still groggy, she sits. “I’m going to the wall.” I follow her outside. As she goes to relieve herself, I look for the water Neene has prepared. The bowl is wide and the water swirls. Crouching down, I pour it into my hands. Rivulets of clear liquid trickle through my fingers as I rub my skin. By the time I’ve washed my face, Awa stands beside me, still in her nightshift. She pours too much over her hands and it spills, darkening a patch of earth. After completing the washing of my face and head, I rub the dirt and pebbles from my feet and ankles and then slip my toes into my sandals. I move around the hut to stand facing Mecca. I am the first in position. A dog barks once from somewhere close. Beyond the bark, there’s another sound but I can’t make out what it is. It’s still dark; moonlight reveals nothing. He reaches out, pulls her arm out to the side. Within moments, he nods. Something deep inside of me cracks when Awa screams and tries to run toward Neene. The rope won’t let her. Neene calls our names, over and over and over, as they bind her wrists again and lead her away from us. I can still hear her screaming even when she’s swallowed by the crowd. My mind blanks. Your sister, Aïssata! I nod to myself, moving closer to Awa. She is shouting, “Where is she? Where is she, Aïssata?” Tears spill from over my nose and into my mouth. The men look over at us and fear explodes. Don’t look up, don’t look up. “Shh shh,” I whisper frantically. “Look down, look down, Awa, please.” And something hot and awful blooms inside me. A knowing. Panic swells until I feel like I’m going to explode like the gunshots did in the village. I drop my head as low as I can and lift the rope. When I feel the pendant hanging from my neck, I curl my fingers around its edges and yank, fast and hard, until the cord snaps. Beads fall. Awa’s fingers close around it before I tell her to take it. Boots. Awa doesn’t scream when he pulls her. But I do. My whole body starts shaking and I rush forward, as far as the rope will let me and, when it pulls me back, I go to my knees. Fire. My whole body feels like someone took a torch to it. I can’t see for the tears. They make me angry because I need to see where she goes. I need to see who takes her, but I don’t see. All I see is Awa. Her hair isn’t in cornrows anymore. Fuzzy curls spring by her ears; her nightshift is covered in dust, dirt and more. I stare at her, screaming her name until my throat hurts. I shift and something hard rolls against my knee. One of the blue beads. Dirtied by earth, I pick it up, frozen, unable to look away. Don’t look up, don’t look up. The bead changes colors depending on where I look: some spots are smeared with tan streaks of dirt; others are almost clear. I use my thumb to roll it against my first finger. “Stand up and walk.” Where is she? Heat swells in my body again; my hands curl. They look at hands. Quick, while I walk, I cover my mouth, parting my lips and slipping the blue bead between them. It clicks against my teeth as I bury it beneath my tongue. The man standing in front of me is tall. His skin is dark, like mine, but with hints of olive. He stares at me and I cannot read his eyes: they are dark but they don’t have my starburst lines. I can’t see light in them. He does not move or speak. But he watches me like no one has ever done. He cocks his head to the side, walks around me. He steps close. He smells different. Tobacco and river. He holds his palm out, turns it over, nods at me. I do what the others have done: hold my arms out, straight in front of me, turn my palms over. He steps even closer, bares his teeth at me, pointing to his own mouth. I smile, wondering what he thinks about the gap between my teeth. When two of his fingers reach out, I jerk back, but he captures my chin and turns my head to the left. Neene gripped my chin. “Run!” I can’t. When he turns my head to the other side, looking at every inch of my face, something I’ve never felt rushes over me. It’s cold and the shaking grows worse. I press my tongue down against the bead. The man moves his head close, staring at my eyes. I stop breathing. He lowers his gaze slowly, dragging it over my neck and shoulders until my teeth rattle. That’s when I see it. Just beyond him, the white tent. It flutters into a gazelle running fast, its white neck stretched long. Its coat is the same tawny color of the golden dirt at home; its white belly soft as a cloud. Two long, ribbed horns stand proudly between its ears. And he runs. My chest opens; the bubbles pop one by one until air fills my lungs. I can feel the wind against my skin, blowing through my uncombed, unbraided hair. He leaps over a large puddle. While he’s suspended in mid-air, long, thin legs reaching for the safe side, it’s like he flies. The birds don’t sing. The frogs don’t splash into the current. Everything holds its breath. When his front legs strike the earth, it shakes. Then his back legs touch down. And then he’s off again, running, running, running and nobody knows where he’s going. Around him, there is only sand and patches of earth overturned. The sound of laughter confuses me. I try to stay with the gazelle, but my vision clears just as my arms drop to my sides. My arms drop to my sides . The muscles hurt to move. Carefully, I roll my shoulder and lift my arm. It really is free of the rope. Somehow, I’m sitting beneath shade, watching the man with the good teeth and clean hands talk to someone else, point to me. The tents are farther away now. I watch the crowds from a hill and scan the faces for Awa. “Scars of Victory: A Memoir” by Julie Wainwright CW : abuse, rape Everyone has a story to tell, and I suppose many of them are pretty much the same. We deal with good and bad, with pain and pleasure, with the good and the not-so-good. Such is life. It’s not easy and not for the faint of heart. It’s about forging on, surviving, and then some. What I mean is that there is more to life than survival. Animals can survive, but humans can thrive and excel beyond trauma. Yes, I’ve had a tough life, marked by physical and emotional violence, yet also by incredible resilience. God instructs the heart through pain and contradictions. I am one of the fortunate ones, having made it through with maturity, confidence, and a passion for life. Help was there when I needed it. Help was there when I asked for it. A good friend once told me that a healthy person will ask for help. I agree. And I am proud to stand among the healthy ones. I had a lot of childhood trauma, but somehow found the inner strength to endure. I live in a small town in Georgia, where everyone knows everyone else and either knows, suspects, or gossips about their neighbors’ dark family secrets. I have far too many hearts to protect to focus on my own. For my story, I changed names, places, and occupations. Those do not matter. What matters are the emotions that consumed me, nearly destroyed me, and eventually led to my salvation. My dad owned his own business, a small farm supply store. To support our family of six, he worked late into the evenings and was not home very much. When he was not home, horrible things happened. I guess bad things happen like that when there is no family authority, and children are vulnerable to violent predators and sadistic tormentors. Many people choose to numb their pain with drugs and alcohol or through addictive behaviors like sex, eating, shopping, or having numerous relationships. I didn’t do that, but I found ways to numb myself. In my most private self, I shut down when I’m hurt or overwhelmed. I’ve always done this since I was a young child. I’ve always been independent and strong. I had to be. I started working at 15 and bought my first car, a 1984 Mustang GT, at 16. I left home at 17. That was the easy part. It felt so good to be independent and rely only on myself. I always had the confidence to pursue my goals and develop what I truly believe is my most incredible gift—the gift of connecting with people, listening and understanding, and expressing empathy. I am a Registered Nurse. At work, Nurse Julie is very assertive and outspoken. It doesn’t matter whether the situation involves staff or a patient. I’m assertive if need be. I can stand in front of a crowd and teach a class with confidence. Empathy and compassion led me to nursing school. I wanted to help others and be there for them, perhaps because of the love that I lacked in my childhood. Peace and love are all I want. I was taught that I was responsible for creating a beautiful life, and I let go of all drama many, many years ago. I spent years quietly stepping away from spaces and relationships that drained my energy, attending support and grief counseling groups, and reading self-help books. All of this helped transform me into a strong, independent, and exciting human being who is grounded, connected, and loved. I love life. I love people. I love myself. My twin sister, Christina, was also a Registered Nurse and was loved by many. She and my dad were both diagnosed with terminal cancers. My twin and I were inseparable, and I threw myself into caring for her and Dad. They both ended up in the same hospice facility, just months apart. I was with them both when they took their last breath. I was alone with Dad when he passed away in my arms. To the end, I was definitely a daddy’s girl, looking at the world through his kind eyes. Christina fought for ten years against an aggressive cancer called Synovial Cell Carcinoma and underwent a left above-the-knee amputation, almost to the hip. She endured several brain tumors, four craniotomies, and endless years of chemotherapy and radiation. I thought I was prepared when she had to leave us, but I wasn’t. When she passed away, it felt like half my soul was sucked out of me. I grieved heavily for years. I lost my best friend. My mother was an out-of-control alcoholic who mentally and physically traumatized me. She was cold and emotionally distant. Our home didn’t feel safe. I learned to make myself as small and quiet as possible, so I wouldn’t trigger her or bring even more chaos into the home. She did everything she could to destroy my self-esteem and self-image. Her failure to protect me forced me to endure in a house of horror. She beat me daily with a belt. She told me daily that she wished I had never been born. Dad told me that Mom was very jealous of my twin and me since we were born, and being the daddy’s girl of the home, I was her target. She looked at me through hateful eyes. At 12 years old, my brother raped me three separate times. My Mom stood and watched the third time, doing nothing. I threatened to tell Dad, and she said she would kill me. I believed her because of the physical abuse she inflicted on me over the years. At 12, I weighed only 56 pounds, and I was emotionally destroyed. It wasn’t until Christina and I were 25 that I told her what had happened, and she said it happened to her as well. My brother is now 57, with end-stage cirrhosis. I don’t talk to him. I never told my dad what my brother did to me, and neither did Christina, for fear of what he would do. My dad was in the Army. There were guns in the home, and he would have killed my brother. My Dad has been gone for ten years, and I promised him I would take care of my mother. Since Dad’s passing, she had five major surgeries and, at 84, is frail and temperamental. I had several opportunities to place her in a rehabilitation facility, but after each surgery, I broke my promise to Dad and brought her home from the hospital. Even though she was verbally abusive, I gave her care from a clinical perspective, which protected our boundaries. I separated my role as her child from my duties as her caregiver. I treated her as my patient, rather than as my mother, and provided medical support without being overwhelmed by personal grief. But today, as I write these words, I’m alive and in love with myself and the world. It sounds strange, but to reach where I am now, I had to crawl over shards of glass, bleeding from pain and degradation, to make it to the other side. I was taught that I was no more than an animal, a feral one in a world without love. I’m older, wiser, and stronger now, but only after enduring a childhood hell in which I was brainwashed into believing I was a mistake. I wanted to tell my story in a plain, honest voice and trust the truth to be enough. I suppose my story has come full circle: although I was not loved or protected, I was able to provide love and protection in the end. I did not run away from my pain. I embraced it as I created a world of love and safety and a life filled with contemplation and creativity. I love my life, the good and the not-so-good. Life is not perfect, but our attitude can help us navigate the harsh storms. People need people. I have family, friends, and a special friend who believes in me and has changed my life for the better. What is different about me now? My perspective, for one, has changed. I am aware of my past and my present. Both are real, and each carries its own distinctive dollop of pain and misery. Life is like that. Everyone gets burned, and we all feel the pain. I can’t change the past. I didn’t make it happen, and I didn’t want it to happen. But I made it through, and I am safe now. I’m a mature middle-aged woman, and my mother cannot hurt me. I want to share my message. You can make it, too. That’s the message that I want to share. Nothing more. Nothing less. If it’s not the truth, I do not speak it, and the truth will set you free. Understanding Trauma: Insights from “The Body Keeps the Score” Bessel van der Kolk’s groundbreaking book, The Body Keeps the Score: Brain, Mind, and Body in the Healing of Trauma , has become a cornerstone in the understanding of trauma and its profound impact on human beings. This book bridges the gap between science, personal experience, and therapeutic practice, shedding light on how trauma reshapes the body and the mind. It empowers us with a transformative understanding of trauma. Reading this book changed my life and gave me hope that pharmaceutical companies haven’t completely taken over the field of psychology and that there are other ways to heal that have been studied decades ago. Understanding Trauma Van der Kolk begins by defining trauma as not just the events that happened but the lasting effects these events have on the mind and body. Trauma stems from deeply distressing or disturbing experiences that overwhelm an individual’s capacity to cope. He explains that trauma is more than a memory—it’s an ongoing physical and emotional reaction. Survivors of trauma often relive their experiences in vivid ways, sometimes decades after the event. How Trauma Affects the Brain One of the key revelations in The Body Keeps the Score is how trauma alters the brain’s functioning. Van der Kolk discusses three main areas of the brain affected by trauma: The Reptilian Brain (brainstem) is responsible for survival instincts. It becomes overactive in trauma survivors, leading to heightened states of fight, flight, or freeze. The Limbic System : This emotional center of the brain, including the amygdala, becomes hyperactive, causing heightened emotional reactions and difficulty regulating feelings. The Prefrontal Cortex : Often referred to as the “rational brain,” this area shuts down under trauma, impairing the ability to think logically and self-regulate. Van der Kolk illustrates how trauma keeps the brain stuck in a state of alarm, which explains the overwhelming emotions, flashbacks, and triggers experienced by survivors. The Body Remembers One of the book’s central ideas is that trauma is stored in the body. Van der Kolk emphasizes that physical sensations, muscle tension, and autonomic nervous system responses often carry the imprint of traumatic experiences. Survivors might not consciously recall their trauma, but their bodies frequently relive it through chronic pain, digestive issues, autoimmune disorders, or other physical symptoms. For example, someone who has experienced assault might flinch at physical touch, or a survivor of war might feel a constant state of hypervigilance. These bodily reactions are ways the body remembers and protects itself from perceived threats. The Role of Dissociation Van der Kolk highlights dissociation as a common coping mechanism for trauma survivors. Dissociation occurs when individuals detach from their physical and emotional experiences to survive overwhelming situations. While helpful now, it often leads to long-term disconnection from one’s body and emotions. Many trauma survivors report feelings of numbness, a sense of unreality, or even memory loss surrounding the traumatic event. This disconnection can make recovery challenging, as it impedes the integration of traumatic memories. Healing Trauma: The Mind-Body Connection Van der Kolk’s book is not just about understanding trauma but also about healing it. He advocates for a holistic approach that addresses both the mind and body. Traditional talk therapy, while valuable, is often insufficient for deeply entrenched trauma. Instead, he suggests incorporating body-focused and experiential therapies. Key modalities discussed include: Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR): EMDR uses guided eye movements to help individuals process and integrate traumatic memories. Yoga and Body Awareness: Trauma disrupts the connection between the mind and body. Yoga helps survivors regain control over their bodies and fosters a sense of safety. Neurofeedback: By training the brain to regulate itself, neurofeedback can help reduce symptoms of trauma, such as anxiety and hypervigilance. Theater and Expressive Arts: Creative outlets like acting allow survivors to express and process emotions in a safe environment. Mindfulness and Meditation: These practices promote present-moment awareness, helping survivors reduce stress and reconnect with their bodies. The Importance of Relationships in Healing Van der Kolk emphasizes the pivotal role of safe and supportive relationships in trauma recovery. Trauma often stems from interpersonal violations, and healing requires restoring trust and connection. He discusses the importance of empathetic and validating environments, whether through therapists, friends, family, or support groups. This underscores the importance of your support in the recovery process. Trauma in Society The book also explores the broader implications of trauma, particularly its prevalence in marginalized communities and its impact on societal systems such as healthcare, education, and criminal justice. Van der Kolk argues that understanding trauma is essential for creating compassionate systems that support healing rather than perpetuating harm. The Body Keeps the Score is more than a book—it’s a call to action. Van der Kolk’s work underscores the importance of recognizing trauma in individual lives and society. By acknowledging the profound ways trauma affects the body and brain, we open the door to innovative and compassionate approaches to healing. Whether you’re a trauma survivor, a caregiver, or a mental health professional, Van der Kolk’s insights provide a roadmap for understanding and addressing the long-lasting effects of trauma. The message is clear: healing is not just a possibility; it’s a reality, and it begins with honoring the connection between the body, mind, and soul. This instills a sense of hope and optimism in the journey of recovery. Key Takeaways Trauma Lives in the Body: The body holds onto trauma, often manifesting through physical symptoms and automatic responses. The Brain’s Role: Trauma rewires the brain, keeping survivors in a state of hyperarousal and emotional reactivity. Healing Requires Integration: Recovery involves reconnecting the mind and body and integrating traumatic memories in a way that no longer dominates a survivor’s life. Holistic Approaches Are Essential: Combining traditional psychotherapy with body-focused modalities offers the most effective path to healing. Passing on this info from my therapist that I have found helpful to know. When you're having a panic attack you don't 'need to breathe'. You specifically need to breathe out. You are feeling pain because you have been breathing too shallowly and have built up too much carbon dioxide. You need to get rid of that. So you need to breathe out for longer than you are breathing in. Breathe out as long as you can, and then let your body be in charge of breathing in. Your body can, and will, do that bit for you. Repeat that as long as you feel you need. Then once you're calmer and aren't feeling the pain you can do the second thing they taught me. Imagine the air lazily entering your body and moving down to curl around in your stomach like a kitten, and then stretching up to move up and out again. This image can help to breathe deeply and slowly again. You can find a different image if another is more useful to you. Repeat as long as you like. # PanicAttack

A Panic Attack May Not Be What You Think I’m going to explain to you what a panic attack is. It does not just mean experiencing a great fear or being terrified irrespective of circumstances. I’ve experienced two bouts of panic attacks in my life. I had to take Xanax to counter the attacks until time worked its magic, and the attacks ceased. A panic attack is not a feeling of panic in the face of a real danger . If you feel something is threatening is happening, and you feel panic, this is a normal response to the threat . If you can remove the threat, and your panic subsides, this is also the sign that what you are experiencing is not a panic attack. “I was watching this thing on TV and I felt I was having a panic attack. Then I turned the TV off, and I was okay.” What you were experiencing wasn’t a panic attack, it was a normal reaction to something your brain found threatening, out there, in the world. See, a panic attack is an irrational sense of fear, when there is nothing out there that can ostensibly harm you. There is nothing that you can remove from your environment to make the panic go away. A panic attack is your body thinking that there’s a threat, when there is no threat. No amount of reassurance will make the panic attack go away, because it is irrational. Join Us Bonfire Merch A panic attack is very different from the first scenario I gave you above, because there is nothing short of taking medicines that will make it go away. Breathing exercises and moderate it, but they won’t eliminate it. How do I know? Again, I’ve had two bouts of panic attacks. I could look around me, and see there was nothing threatening in my environment, but my sense of panic did not go away. I could reason that there was no threat, but this rationality found no purchase in the irrationality of the panic attack. “But I was able to make my panic go away with…” If it was anything short of taking an anxiolytic, what you experienced was plain old panic , and not a panic attack . Using the incorrect language, and insisting that your plain old panic is a panic attack, is harmful in much the same that insisting that someone who experiences a bout of anxiety on a date is suffering from social anxiety, or that someone who is sad at the death of a pet is experiencing depression. People normally rebound from their anxiety or their sadness. One sure sign that what you are dealing with is not social anxiety or depression is that you can easily fix the problem. People with social anxiety, for instance, will ruminate before and after the event. People experiencing depression won’t be pulled out of depression by a joke. It is harmful in the same way that saying “we’re all a little autistic” is harmful. It is a way to minimize a real problem, a problem that cannot be merely fixed by reorganizing your world. anxiety AutisticWriters danger irrational minimization panic PanicAttack YourAutisticLife

Is there really a bright side? “Always Look on the Bright Side of Life”, was coined in 1979 by Eric Idle, for the ending of the Monty Python film; Life of Brian. Sang by another man facing crucifixion in attempt to cheer up the main character, Brian, the song features lyrics that have a surprisingly deep message. In a full-circle way, the song repeats the same themes; the unfortunate parts of life, picking yourself up, and focusing on the good. Which, for a comedic and incredibly satirical film, is something we should all deeply consider. But what if there actually isn’t a bright side? Personally, I struggle a lot to remain optimistic. So much so, that 2 months ago, I got a tattoo with the phrase ‘Amor Fati’, meaning ‘Love Fate’ in Latin. But the fact I felt the need to get the tattoo alone goes to show how sometimes we do need reminders that things will work out. It’s easy to say as a pessimist, but it’s incredibly difficult to remain optimistic all the time. It’s human to have emotions and have bad days, but the most important skill to have is ‘to look on the bright side’. Although, on the flip side, we have to be wary of toxic positivity. Think of it this way: Yes, things probably will work out, and yes, it’s always beneficial to focus on the good, but it’s also important to take time to actually feel . Perhaps it’s naive to say, but I truly don’t believe we should always look for the good in a situation. I don’t believe in suppressing feelings, hiding from the truth, or ignoring problems. If we do that, how on earth do we expect to learn or move on from them? I think it’s a very human thing to do; seeing the good in the bad. And I applaud those who are able to do so. But what do we actually gain in doing so? That isn’t to say, however, that we should dwell in the bad things that happen to us – it just means we should allow ourselves to actually feel waht we’re feeling and heal, rather than make excuses and move on too quickly. And in another realm, this toxic thinking can lead us to not only dismiss our own feelings, but also the feelings of others. It can seem a simple remark, saying “don’t worry about that job turning you down, there’ll be another one”, but in reality, we’re just affirming that instead of moving forward, we’re actually moving past the issue. It’s more beneficial here, to ask your friend what they thought lead to that outcome, what could be done better, how has it left them feeling. Rather than dismissing the situation and encouraging them to dive head first into another (possibly negative) instance. This can be a very confusing topic, because ideally, we need to find a balance of the two. We need to find a way to allow ourselves to feel and accept outcomes, but also remain positive that things can move forward from it. We can’t dismiss, but we can’t dwell. We have to accept, and use it to push us forward. This is a very interesting topic to me, and something I personally struggle with, so look out for more posts with this theme: accepting outcomes . If I Had Legs I’d Kick You: Another Brilliant Psychological Drama 🦵 Written and directed by Mary Bronstein, If I Had Legs I’d Kick You is an excellent 2025 psychological drama starring Rose Byrne. A challenging film about mental health struggles, it explores the lead character’s descent into major instability. The plot is driven along by the brilliance of Rose Byrne, quite the performance in a very challenging piece. It follows a mother stretched to her psychological limits dealing with work, an absent husband, and young daughter struggling with an illness. There’s Never Enough Wine in If I Had Legs I’d Kick You Over two hours this is quite the slow burner, with Rose Byrne’s character Linda allowed the time for a realistic sense of mental decline. Byrne is probably most famous for her role as a Little Miss Perfect type in Kristen Wiig’s Bridesmaids (2011). At 47, this is her first notable serious acting role, which kind of highlights how difficult it is for actors to get a role worthy of their talents. As she’s goddamn awesome in this. A hell of a performance. The narrative follows Linda as she gradually loses it, descending further and further into a world of stress and mental instability. She works as a psychotherapist, with her husband Charles (Christian Slater) working away from home as a ship’s captain. Meanwhile, her daughter has a feeding disorder and is anxiety-ridden. Linda seems to be aware she’s stressed, but in denial about the true extent, but is nevertheless seeking counsel in her therapist colleague (an unexpected serious turn by Conan O’Brien). You never see the daughter, all you ever hear is her clingy voice, screams, and general protestations. The struggles with this, including driving her daughter daily to the hospital, then to school, whilst also managing her day job, is capped off when her apartment’s roof collapses and is flooded. This catalogue of problems reminds us of the Coen brother’s excellent A Serious Man (2009) and the consideration of how the hell everything can go wrong at once. Facing exhaustion through stress and lack of sleep, she’s also drinking wine heavily every night and smoking weed. These don’t help and her behaviour becomes increasingly unstable. Some elements of the story become surrealist. There’s a scene with a newly bought pet hamster that makes you question reality, as if Linda is so exhausted she’s hallucinating things. That’s certainly the case at times as it’s made clear she’s imagining some occurrences. Other times, the audience is left guessing what’s going on. Such as with the open-ended nature of the film’s conclusion, where the peak of Linda’s mania arrives. We should imagine many mothers who watch If I Had Legs I’d Kick You will relate to it enormously. It’s not outright a feminist text, we’d argue, it’s more a naturalistic focus on one woman’s battle with rapidly declining mental health. There aren’t any answers provided for what Linda should do, more it’s an accurate depiction of how someone can lose control. And in that depiction, people can find that all-important relatable solace. Not that If I Had Legs I’d Kick You is a miserable experience. There are lashings of excellent dark humour and absurdist happenings, but it really is Rose Byrne’s fantastic performance that should get you watching the thing. The Production of If I Had Legs I’d Kick You The ever-excellent American independent company A24 led this production. They’re responsible for backing so many modern classics and here’s another. The film got its debut at the Sundance 2025 Film Festival and launched in February 2025 across international cinemas. It didn’t get a huge distribution as we can’t recall seeing it advertised here in the UK. But it did well enough to make $1.7 million at the box office off its limited budget. It launched on Blu-ray and DVD in December 2025 (reminder to us, we need to get a copy). Rose Byrne’s performance got huge swathes of praise. She was nominated for Best Actress at the 2026 Oscars and won the same award at various other festivals and awards ceremonies this year. Don’t straight! She deserved it. The most notable win was probably the Golden Globe Awards gong. From our counting, Byrne has won 15 awards for her performance so far! It really does carry the film. With a script like this, you need someone to deliver and she did it big time. Although Bronstein’s screenplay was very sharp and well written, too (just everything about the film is dominated by Byrne). The plot was based on Bronstein’s struggles dealing with her severely ill 7-year-old daughter. If I Had Legs I’d Kick You was shot in August and September of 2023 in Montauk of New York. Mary Bronstein waived her director’s fee to add just two extra days to the shoot, which was only 27 days long. A reminder that many in the film industry don’t earn that much, it’s only the big hitters who rake it in. Some are just there for the love of it. The Nuanced Manners In Which Regular Chronic Stress Impacts Your Brain and Body The exam worth 75% of your grade looms large over your hnead. The impending doom of getting home 30 minutes late when your mother said 10:00 PM sharp. The Homecoming game in 2 days against the best defense in the entire state. Your first driving test with the instructor who historically fails everybody. No…these are not killing your brain. Actually, these natural responses may prove vital in heightening your ability to perform, rendering you alert and focused during the task, drowning out potential distractions. However, what about a state of chronic stress? The constant thought of being let gone by your boss leering like a rain cloud in the back of your mind. The fact that your relationship is hanging on by a thread and you’ve just forgotten the date of your anniversary and are afraid to ask. The class you signed up for in optimism, now presenting itself as the most difficult scientific entity of the past few centuries. Are these responses vital? Perhaps. But, are they healthy? That’s up to us to study In the modern world, Chronic Stress is sadly treated as collateral damage that naturally accompanies a hustler’s lifestyle, a go-getter mentality, or a co-requisite of ambition. While some levels of daily stress in intervals are normal and can actually keep us alert and sharp, Chronic Stress that looms over your mind in completely irrelevant situations can do permanent, sometimes irreversible damage before any signs and symptoms are noticed. Hence, it is crucial to educate ourselves on the potential damage so we actively train our minds to prevent ourselves from going down an endless hill © ChatGPT, 2026 The Wonders Of Worry Blending Colors Stress is quite a multi-faceted topic, nearly impossible to examine without understanding how its components blend together. Playing to our strengths, we’ll first zero in on the primary neural centers involved in the stress response and their sequence-based involvement, and transition into the molecular components. So, of course, the first step involves recognition. When the brain processes sensory inputs, the input follows two different ‘roads.’ The first road involves Thalamic input directly to the Amygdala, known as the ‘Low Road,’ which operates on a ~12 ms timescale. The second involves Thalamic input projected to the Cortex, which then reaches the Amygdala, known as the ‘High Road,’ which operates on a ~30-40 ms timescale. The difference between the two paths is the amount of context they carry. Both have advantages in terms of the speed at which the Low Road transmits information, and the amount of information the High Road carries. Now, as this input makes its way to the Amygdala, specifically the Basolateral Amygdala, we have to call upon one more friend (who we’re no stranger to)…the Hippocampus! As cortical (High Road) input makes its way to the Amygdala, it’s not as if this input is totally isolated. A similar fear-based experience has likely occurred before. Stored hippocampal with certain similarities can actually fire if the incoming sensory input somewhat matches the context under which the previous memory was formed. If the context matches the current event, it increases the probability that the BLA will fire downstream. But, what does it fire to? Spoiler Alert: This is a comprehensive outline of the general Amygdala Network, in terms of relevant areas it receives input from, and the functional outputs that it produces. Notice the type of outputs that are produced, mostly relevant in emotional context © ScienceDirect Zhang et al 2021 Where’s The Switch While we’ve outlined how stressful experiences reach our cognitive centers from a processing standpoint, it doesn’t end our discussion of the neural cascade that results in that eerily familiar chilling of the skin, raising of the hair, and speeding of the heart. See, the Basolateral Amygdala may be responsible for determining what actually gets filtered to be a ‘threat,’ but it’s the ‘Switch’ alluded to in the title of this section that allows us to consciously respond to the stimulus as a threat. This Switch is known as the Central Amygdala, which directly receives projections from the BLA. The Central Amygdala is the primary effector responsible for triggering the widespread, classical ‘fight-or-flight’ response. It may strike you as a potential surprise, but the Central Amygdala actually doesn’t have a classical role in the processing of threat from a cognitive sense. The Central Amygdala’s principal duty is as an intermediary hub in order to regulate the function of the Autonomic Nervous System, projecting to a structure which has been harped down the throats of neuroscientists, endocrinologists, and biologists alike. A structure responsible for a heavy portion of many physiological responses…you likely have already predicted correctly…the Hypothalamus (along with some other, potentially new friends). Fight or Flight The Hypothalamus is introduced relatively early in Neuroscientific discussions due to its versatile role in, well, many hormonally regulated processes, sleep and sexual drive not being the least prominent. However, our focus shifts to stress. At this point in our journey, a stressful stimulus has been recognized and input has reached the Central Amygdala, the output region. Remember, we’re still dealing with Acute Stress, NOT Chronic Stress. Within the Central Amygdala are 2 subdivisions, the Lateral (CeL) and Medial (CeM). If an aversive stimulus reaches the CeA, the CeL has populations of neurons known as CRF and SOM∂, and SOM∂ inhibits the CeM. However, upon arrival, the stimulus can activate CRF, which inhibits SOM∂, and in a ‘double negative,’ reverses the inhibition of the CeM, and activates the CeA as a whole. Now, we must transition primarily to the CeM, and the famous pathway that everyone associates stress with. The HPA Axis. The Centromedial Amygdala, now ready to fire, has many output points, but we’re specifically focused on the Hypothalamus (no shocker), which contains the Paraventricular Nucleus. The PVN releases Corticotropin Releasing Factor (CRF, colloquially), onto the Anterior Pituitary Gland. Hint hint, one of the first things we’re taught is about how the Hypothalamus often projects onto the Pituitary! The A.P releases Adrenocorticotropic Hormone onto the Adrenal Cortex, which releases Glucocorticoids…and these little guys form the basis of the entire next section Although definitely not needed for this particular topic, this is a comprehensive list of the major Hypothalamic Hormones. Notice that the Hypothalamic Hormones aren’t independent agents; they’re all relying on some form of downstream signaling to relay the message, because the Hypothalamic Hormones can either Stimulate or Inhibit release of further Hormones. Not everything which is released automatically has an amplifying effect…in many cases, as we will assuredly see below, it’s actually quite the opposite. © ChatGPT, 2026 Don’t Lose Sleep Self-Servicing Traffic Light Fittingly, in the second section of the article, we move to Chronic Stress. It was obviously crucial to understand what contributes to our stress response, specifically Glucocorticoid release, but we have to now stop tunneling our thinking towards Acute Stress alone. Glucocorticoids come into play a minimum of 15-30 minutes after the stressor. So, why are they significant? It’s because Glucocorticoids, quite literally, are power-hungry. Let’s first focus on how they regulate themselves, and then their systemic regulation, because these sub-sections are going to be doozies. Interestingly, enough, while Glucocorticoids elevate during episodes of Stress, they themselves are actually responsible for initiating mechanisms which ‘calm’ the Stress Response post-stimulus. Of course, this does not occur right away; suppressing the fear response during an actual stressor is dangerous for…various reasons. However, when the Glucocorticoid concentration is elevated, it controls the Stress Response on short and long time scales. Pituitary Glucocorticoid Receptors which are occupied and hence activated are responsible for actually decreasing ACTH production, resulting in a ‘partial brake’ effect. Furthermore, the elevation of Glucocorticoids upregulates expression of FPKB51 (I know, they just make names up). FPKB51, however, does not serve some alien-like function; it actually does something quite practical. It alters the configuration of the binding pocket of the Glucocorticoid Receptor so that binding does not occur perfectly, and the stress response is somewhat controlled. On a long-term scale, around hours or even days, Glucocorticoids function to return the Hippocampal-PVN Axis back to baseline. The Hippocampus does not normally excite the PVN. In quite the opposite fashion, it consistently inhibits it at a physiological state of rest. Through Genetic regulation, Glucocorticoids assist in the expression of factors which downregulate ACTH/CRF Synthesis and the overall sensitivity to the Stress Response, returning the brain to a state of rest. But, what happens if that rest never comes? Chronically Offline Just to be clear, I might have made it sound like Glucocorticoids weaken the Stress response. No, that’s not what they do. They regulate the stress response. Although that involves playing a role in the process of cooling the Stress Response, they also play a large role in elevating it. It is because of Glucocorticoids, in conjunction with Norepinephrine (Adrenaline), that stressful memories are so well remembered. It is because of Glucocorticoids that we have such a robust energy response to the stressor, and why we feel so drained after the experience. Glucocorticoids are responsible for increasing Receptor expression of Adrenaline-Responding Receptors, which is why our heart can feel as if it’s pounding out of the very chest cavity that houses it. You can start to see why keeping Glucocorticoid concentration elevated by remaining chronically stressed is so dangerous. But, the acute stress response isn’t actually the main reason why Chronic Stress is highlighted as so dangerous. The real ‘poison’ that we mentioned in the title comes from rather Chronic events rather than acute sensations of stress Persistently elevated Glucocorticoid levels, a sign of Chronic or unresolved Stress, causes Cellular, Molecular, and Systemic damage that we may not even be aware of until the damage is frighteningly noticeable. While we won’t outline every single molecular pathway, there are some absolutely key consequences we must be aware of. Molecularly, the major consequence is the suppression of BDNF, a big name even in the non-neuroscientific community. BDNF is an all-around growth molecule, scientifically called a ‘Trophic Factor.’ The suppression of this molecule leads to a decreased ability to learn new things, create new neurons, form new neural connections, and maintain existing ones. Molecularly, you destroy the very framework of what made your brain so special…its ability to consistently rewire itself Cellularly, over a sufficient time period, elevated Glucocorticoid levels will eventually result in cell death in the Hippocampus; and neural death is not like other apoptosis, because neurons essentially do not regenerate. The circuit is tainted forever. And, Systemically, it doesn’t stop. Chronic Cortisol (the primary Glucocorticoid) elevation results in a lessened default Hippocampal inhibition of the HPA Axis, and it can feel like everything gets you angry. The Prefrontal Cortex also suffers from the same ailments as the Hippocampus. Its connections are withered and it undergoes atrophy; your cognition literally fades away. Your ability to control your own self erodes like a decaying banana. You lose your very essence, because your problems became them Intricate, right? The Week I Wish Wasn’t .. I know. I’ve used this header before … A couple of times actually. It’s the only one that accurately describes the week that we’ve just had. On the night of Monday August 3rd, at 10pm we experienced what could only be described as a plumbing emergency. Our toilet decided it’d had enough of this life and finally decided it was time to go to god. So, by 10pm Monday night we had a leaky toilet and no idea how to fix it Tuesday morning, we decided to call a plumber so, at 6.45am I was reaching out to Irwins Plumbing Service for help. To say I / we were stressed was an under statement. We knew it was going to be costly ( We didn’t know how much at the time) and I had to wrangle our finances to ensure we could cover it For those that are not aware, we live in a rental. We’ve lived in this rental since 2001. Mid 2002 the unit was sold ( We went with it) and our new/ current landlord gave us a lease for 12 months. That lease expired in November 2003. Since then, we’ve been on a month by month basis and as such our landlord has not done so much as a property inspection or performed any routine maintenance. In fact, asking him to do so is like pulling teeth ( aka nigh on impossible) so, for the most part, we’ve attempted to fix stuff on our own. By Tuesday afternoon, Carlos from Irwins Plumbing came by to assess the damage and give us a quote to fix it. As predicted it was a costly exercise, nonetheless I arranged to have someone come by on the Thursday of that week to fix it In the interim my my nerves were shot and having the added stress of work being busier than a one legged man in a hopping contest did very little to help matters. Thursday morning hubby and I were up at the god awful time of 4.30am with the promise of a plumber being on site at 7am. Naturally, 7am came and went. By 9.40am I had called Irwins Plumbing to enquire as to our plumbers whereabouts and was told we’d been placed in a window that was in fact between 9am -1pm and we were the next job on the guys list. At 12.49pm Trent entered the chat. Trent as it turns out was our plumber and he was running a little late after being held up at the previous job. He arrived at around 1.15pm and commenced work straight away. It took him all of an hour to fix it and he did a bloody fantastic job! Not only that, when all was said and done, the job came in $104 cheaper than originally quoted – so I was happy with that. Trent, if you ever read this, good job mate! We’re super happy with the work you’ve done! 5 stars to you friend! Despite this, I still wish it was money we didn’t have to spend. We’re now having to put the money back and that means things are going to be a little tight for a while. Ugh! Being an adult sucks balls!
